title: SwiftUI & iOS Engineering
subtitle: Swift, SwiftUI, concurrency, architecture, testing and shipping

modules.title: Swift Language Foundations
modules.summary: Constants, type inference, optionals, collections and closures: the language you'll write in every other module.

blocks.text: Swift is statically typed, but you rarely write the types. The compiler infers them from the right-hand side. Use `let` by default and switch to `var` only when the value really changes. The compiler warns when a `var` is never mutated.

`Array`, `Dictionary` and `String` are value types. Assigning one copies it, conceptually. In practice the copy is deferred until someone mutates it (copy-on-write), so passing arrays around is cheap.

blocks.code:
let machineID = "BBI-0042"          // constant, inferred String
var trayCount = 6                     // variable, inferred Int
let price: Decimal = 49.50            // explicit type: money is never Double

var trays = ["A1", "A2"]
var snapshot = trays                  // a copy (storage shared until mutation)
snapshot.append("A3")
print(trays.count, snapshot.count)    // 2 3

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Using `Double` for prices. 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3 in binary floating point. Use `Decimal` or integer paise.
`let` on a class instance makes the *reference* constant. The object's properties can still change.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: What does `let` guarantee for a struct versus a class instance?
An optional is an enum with two cases, `.none` and `.some(value)`. The compiler forces you to handle the missing case before you use the value, and that removes a whole class of null crashes.
Use `guard let` for preconditions at the top of a function, `if let` for a branch, `??` for defaults and optional chaining (`?.`) for walking through optional properties.
Pitfalls

items: Force unwrapping (`!`) crashes when the value is nil. Keep it for values you've proven exist, such as a literal URL in a test.
Implicitly unwrapped optionals (`String!`) hide the same crash behind normal-looking code.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: How is `Optional` implemented, and what does optional chaining return?

Most data shaping in an app is a pipeline: filter what you need, transform it, then group or sum it. `map`, `filter`, `reduce`, `compactMap` and `Dictionary(grouping:by:)` express that without manual loops or index bookkeeping.
Key paths such as `\.name` can stand in for a closure that reads a property. That keeps pipelines short and readable.

blocks.code:
struct Item { let name: String; let tray: String; let price: Decimal }
let items = [
    Item(name: "Chips", tray: "A", price: 20),
    Item(name: "Juice", tray: "B", price: 45),
    Item(name: "Cookies", tray: "A", price: 30)
]
let total = items.reduce(0) { $0 + $1.price }           // 95
let byTray = Dictionary(grouping: items, by: \.tray)     // ["A": [..2], "B": [..1]]
let cheap = items.filter { $0.price < 40 }.map(\.name)   // ["Chips", "Cookies"]
let codes = ["12", "x", "7"].compactMap(Int.init)        // [12, 7]

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Chaining `.filter`, then `.map`, then `.first` on a huge array builds intermediate arrays. Use `.lazy` or `first(where:)`.
`reduce(into:)` is faster than `reduce` when the accumulator is a collection.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: What is the difference between `map`, `compactMap` and `flatMap`?
A closure captures the variables it uses *by reference*. That is why a counter closure can keep incrementing a local that has already gone out of scope.

A closure the function stores or calls later must be marked `@escaping`. Escaping closures are where retain cycles come from (Module 3), so every escaping closure that mentions `self` deserves a second look.
Pitfalls

items: Expecting a closure to see the value from when it was created. Without a capture list it sees the current value.
Marking every parameter `@escaping` out of habit. Non-escaping closures are cheaper and allow implicit `self`.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: When do you need `@escaping`, and what does a capture list change?

lessons.title: Error handling: throws, Result and typed throws

blocks.text: Errors in Swift are values that conform to `Error`. A function that can fail is marked `throws`, every call to it is marked `try`, and `do`/`catch` handles the failure. `try?` turns an error into `nil` and `try!` crashes on one, so use `try!` only where failure is impossible.

Typed throws (Swift 6) let a function declare exactly which error type it throws, such as `throws(PaymentError)`. Use it for closed, internal domains like payments inside one module. Keep untyped `throws` for public APIs that may grow new failure cases. At the UI edge, map errors to messages a person can act on.
Pitfalls

items: `try?` on something you should log. The reason for the failure disappears.
One catch-all “Something went wrong” message. Distinguish errors the user can fix, such as topping up the wallet, from ones they can't.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: When would you use typed throws, and when would you avoid them?

lessons.title: Enums, associated values and pattern matching

blocks.text: Enums model a closed set of possibilities. Raw values map cases to wire formats. Associated values carry data that belongs to one case only. Because `switch` must be exhaustive, adding a case makes the compiler list every place that needs updating.
Pattern matching goes beyond `switch`. `where` clauses add conditions, tuple patterns decide on two values at once, and `if case` and `for case` match a single case without a full switch.
Pitfalls

items: `default:` in a switch over your own enum. New cases fall into it silently instead of failing to compile.
Passing raw strings such as `"door_open"` around the app. Convert to an enum at the boundary.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: Why avoid default in a switch over your own enum?

modules.title: Types, Protocols & Generics
modules.summary: Value vs reference semantics, protocol-oriented design, and generics with some and any.

lessons.title: struct, class, enum and actor: choosing a type

blocks.text: The choice is about semantics. A `struct` is copied, so each owner has its own value. A `class` is shared, so everyone holding a reference sees the same object. An `enum` models a fixed set of states. An `actor` is a reference type that serialises access to its mutable state.

Default to structs for models and view state. Reach for a class when you need shared identity, such as a socket session or a UIKit subclass, and for an actor when that shared state is touched concurrently.

blocks.code:
struct CartLine { var qty: Int }          // value: copied on assign
final class Session { var qty = 0 }       // reference: shared

var a = CartLine(qty: 1); var b = a; b.qty = 5
print(a.qty)    // 1

let s1 = Session(); let s2 = s1; s2.qty = 5
print(s1.qty)   // 5

enum ConnectionState {
    case idle, scanning
    case connected(machineID: String)
    case failed(Error)
}

actor TokenStore {
    private var token: String?
    func set(_ t: String) { token = t }   // callers must await this
}

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: A struct that holds a class reference is only shallowly copied. Both copies share the object.
Methods that change a struct's properties need `mutating`, and you can't call them on a `let`.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: When would you pick a class over a struct in a SwiftUI app?
Protocols describe capabilities. Extensions give those capabilities default behaviour. Types opt in by conforming, instead of inheriting from a base class, and that works for structs and enums too.
Only methods declared in the protocol body dispatch dynamically. A method that exists only in an extension is chosen by the variable's *static* type, which is a classic interview trap.
Pitfalls

items: Adding a method only in an extension and expecting a conformer's own version to win when called through the protocol type.
Protocols with dozens of requirements. Split them so fakes in tests stay small.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: Explain static vs dynamic dispatch for protocol extension methods.

Generics let one function work over many types while keeping full type information. `some P` is an opaque type: one concrete type, chosen by the implementation and hidden from the caller, with no runtime box. `any P` is an existential: a box that can hold different conforming types at runtime, at the cost of dynamic dispatch.
Rule of thumb from WWDC22: write `some` first and switch to `any` only when you really need a mix of types in one collection or property.
Pitfalls

items: Returning `some View` from two branches that produce different types. Wrap them in `@ViewBuilder` instead.
Using `any` everywhere out of habit. Every call then goes through a witness table.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: Compare `some` and `any`. What does each cost at runtime?

The compiler synthesises `Equatable`, `Hashable` and `Codable` when every stored property already conforms. Write them by hand only when you have a reason. If you write `==`, `hash(into:)` must use exactly the same fields, or `Set` and `Dictionary` misbehave.

`Identifiable` and `Equatable` answer different questions. Identity asks which thing this is, which SwiftUI uses to match rows. Equality asks whether the value changed, which tells SwiftUI whether to redraw. Don't define `==` by id alone, or a changed price can look unchanged.
Pitfalls

items: Equality by id only. SwiftUI and your tests can no longer tell when a value changed.
A class in a `Set` whose hash depends on mutable fields. Mutating it strands it in the wrong bucket.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: What's the difference between Identifiable and Equatable, and why does SwiftUI care about both?

A property wrapper packages storage behaviour behind `@Name`. It provides `wrappedValue` and, optionally, a `projectedValue` that you reach with `$`. `@State` and `@AppStorage` use the same machinery, except their storage lives in SwiftUI or UserDefaults instead of in your struct.

A result builder turns a list of statements, including `if` and `for`, into one value. That's how `@ViewBuilder` builds views. Macros such as `@Observable` and `@Model` are different: they generate code at compile time, and you can right-click and expand them in Xcode to read what they add.
Pitfalls

items: Hiding expensive work, such as disk reads, behind a property wrapper's getter.
Confusing macros with wrappers. `@Observable` rewrites the class at compile time. It doesn't wrap a single property.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: How does @State differ from a property wrapper you write yourself?

modules.title: Memory Management & ARC
modules.summary: Reference counting, retain cycles, weak vs unowned and copy-on-write.

blocks.text: ARC inserts retain and release calls at compile time and frees an object when its strong count reaches zero. It is not a garbage collector, so it can't break cycles. A cycle forms when A strongly holds B and B strongly holds A.

The most common iOS cycle: a view model owns a socket, the socket stores a callback closure, and that closure captures the view model strongly. Neither can reach zero. A `[weak self]` capture list breaks it.

diagram.title: retain cycle
diagram.caption: Three strong references form a loop, so no reference count reaches zero. Capturing `[weak self]` replaces the highlighted arrow with the dashed one, and `deinit` runs again.

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Using `unowned` when the closure can outlive `self`. Accessing it then crashes.
Block-based `NotificationCenter` observers and repeating `Timer`s that capture `self`. These are the same cycle in disguise.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: Walk through a retain cycle you've fixed and how you proved it was gone.

Standard collections share their storage buffer between copies and duplicate it only when one copy is mutated while the buffer is shared. You can give your own types the same behaviour with `isKnownUniquelyReferenced`.
This is why passing a 10,000-element array into a SwiftUI view is cheap: nothing is copied until someone writes.
Pitfalls

items: Assuming every struct is cheap to copy. A struct with 40 stored properties is copied field by field.
Wrapping a class in a struct without copy-on-write logic. You then get shared mutation behind a value-type facade.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: How does copy-on-write work, and how would you implement it yourself?

lessons.title: Finding leaks with the Memory Graph debugger

blocks.text: To find a leak, repeat the suspect flow (open and close the machine screen five times), then press Debug Memory Graph. Filter by your type name. Five live `MachineHomeViewModel` instances where you expect zero means something is holding them. The graph shows the path of strong references. Turn on Malloc Stack Logging in the scheme's Diagnostics to also see where each object was allocated.

Purple warning markers flag only unreachable cycles. Memory that's still reachable but never used again, such as a growing cache, is abandoned, not leaked. Find it with Instruments Allocations: mark a generation, repeat the flow, mark again, and look at what each generation added.
Pitfalls

items: Trusting the absence of purple markers. Reachable but unused objects never show them.
Checking only on the Simulator. Memory limits and image decoding differ on devices.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: Walk through how you'd prove a view model is leaking.

lessons.title: Stack vs heap and method dispatch

blocks.text: Value types are usually stored inline, on the stack or inside their container, with no reference counting. They move to the heap when an escaping closure captures them, when they're too large for an existential's inline buffer, or when an enum case is `indirect`. Array storage always lives on the heap, even though `Array` is a struct.

Swift dispatches calls in four ways: static for structs, `final`, `private` and extension-only methods; vtable for overridable class methods; witness table for protocol requirements; and Objective-C messaging for `@objc dynamic`. Generics constrained with `some` or `<T>` can be specialised into static calls. Measure with Time Profiler on a Release build before rewriting anything.
Pitfalls

items: Micro-optimising dispatch without a profile. The hot path is usually I/O or layout.
Assuming a struct is always free. A struct holding many reference-type properties pays retain and release costs on every copy.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: When does a Swift struct end up on the heap?

modules.title: SwiftUI Fundamentals
modules.summary: Views as values, modifiers and their order, stacks and the layout handshake.

lessons.title: Views are values: body and modifier order

blocks.text: A SwiftUI view is a cheap struct that *describes* UI. SwiftUI calls `body` whenever a dependency changes, diffs the result and updates the real render tree. Creating views is cheap. Doing heavy work inside `body` is not.
Each modifier wraps the view in a new view, so order matters. Padding then background paints the padded area. Background then padding paints only the text and adds space outside it.
Pitfalls

items: Formatting dates or sorting arrays inside `body` on every render. Do it once, in the model.
Reaching for `AnyView` to silence type errors. It hides identity from SwiftUI's diffing.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: Why does modifier order matter? Give an example where it changes the result.

Layout is a three-step handshake. The parent proposes a size, the child picks its own size, and the parent places the child. Stacks divide their proposal among children. `Spacer` takes whatever is left. `frame` changes the proposal.
Align on text baselines, not centres, whenever text of different sizes sits in one row.
Pitfalls

items: Hard-coding widths that break at large Dynamic Type sizes.
Nesting five stacks where one `Grid` or `LabeledContent` would do.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: Describe SwiftUI's layout process in three steps.

links.title: Stacks, Grids, and Outlines in SwiftUI

lessons.title: Text, images, SF Symbols and Dynamic Type

blocks.text: Text styles such as `.body` and `.headline` scale with the user's Dynamic Type setting, but fixed point sizes don't. Use `@ScaledMetric` to scale spacing and icon sizes with the text, and for a brand font use `Font.custom(_:size:relativeTo:)` so it scales too. Format numbers and dates with format styles such as `.currency` and `.dateTime` instead of building strings by hand.

`Image(systemName:)` sits on the text baseline and scales with the font around it. SF Symbols support rendering modes (`.hierarchical`, `.palette`) and variable values for things like signal strength. `AsyncImage` is fine for a single image, but it has no memory cache of its own, so feeds need an image pipeline (Module 13, lesson 6).
Pitfalls

items: `.font(.system(size: 17))` ignores the user's text size. Use a text style or `relativeTo:`.
Checking only the default size. Test the largest accessibility sizes in previews and let rows wrap with `ViewThatFits`.
Using `AsyncImage` in a long feed. Rows re-download as they scroll back in.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: How do you make a custom font support Dynamic Type?

You can split a long `body` three ways: a computed property, a `@ViewBuilder` function, or a separate `View` struct. Only the struct gives SwiftUI a boundary. Its body runs only when its own inputs change, while a computed property is re-evaluated every time the parent's body runs.

A container that accepts `@ViewBuilder` content lets callers pass any views, including `if` and `ForEach`. Combined with a `ViewModifier`, this is how a design system ships cards, sections and sheets that look the same everywhere.
Pitfalls

items: One 300-line body split into computed properties. It reads better but performs exactly the same.
Passing a whole model into a small subview that only shows one field, which ties it to every change in the model.
Reaching for `AnyView` to return different views. Use `@ViewBuilder`.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: When does extracting a subview struct actually improve performance?

A preview is the fastest feedback loop you have. Write one `#Preview` per state you care about: loaded, empty, offline, error. Pass fake services through the same initialisers production uses. Previews never touch the network, and they double as living documentation of every state.

Check large Dynamic Type, dark mode and small devices from the canvas or with environment overrides. For shared setup, such as an in-memory SwiftData store, iOS 18 adds `PreviewModifier`, which builds the context once and reuses it across previews.
Pitfalls

items: Previews that call the real API. They become slow and flaky, and break offline.
Forgetting environment objects. The preview crashes with the same error a missing injection would cause in production.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: How do you keep previews fast and reliable in a large app?

links.title: Adding previews to your interface files

modules.title: State & Data Flow
modules.summary: @State, @Binding, @Observable, the environment, and how view identity decides state lifetime.

blocks.text: `@State` declares a source of truth that the view owns. SwiftUI keeps it alive across `body` evaluations for as long as the view keeps its identity. Mark it `private` because nothing outside should set it.
`@Binding` gives a child read-write access to state that someone else owns. The `$` prefix turns state into a binding.
Pitfalls

items: Passing a `@State` value down as a plain `let` and wondering why the child's edits don't stick.
Initialising `@State` from an init parameter and expecting later parameter changes to reset it. They don't.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: When do you use `@State`, `@Binding` and a plain property?

The `@Observable` macro (iOS 17) tracks which properties each `body` actually reads. A view re-renders only when one of *those* properties changes. That is finer-grained than `ObservableObject`, where any `@Published` change invalidates every observer.
Own an observable model with `@State`, pass it as a plain `let`, share it with `.environment(model)`, and use `@Bindable` when you need `$model.property` bindings.

diagram.title: dependency tracking
diagram.caption: SwiftUI records which properties each `body` reads. Changing `lines` re-renders only the badge, changing `note` re-renders only the text field, and a view that reads neither never re-renders.

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Using `@StateObject` or `@ObservedObject` with an `@Observable` class. Use `@State` and plain properties.
Typing while `NoteField` is visible re-renders only views that read `note`. If everything re-renders, check what `body` reads.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: How does `@Observable` differ from `ObservableObject` in what it invalidates?

The environment carries two kinds of things down the tree. `@Observable` objects go in with `.environment(object)` and come out with `@Environment(Type.self)`. Plain values use keys, and the `@Entry` macro (Xcode 16) declares a custom key in one line. Children inherit everything set above them.

Use the environment for things many views need: the router, the session, the theme, analytics. Use initialiser injection for a screen's real dependencies so tests and previews must supply them. A missing `@Observable` environment object crashes at runtime, so add it in every preview.
Pitfalls

items: Putting every dependency in the environment. A screen's real requirements become invisible and untestable.
Forgetting the object in a preview or a test host. The result is a crash saying no observable object of that type was found.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: Environment or initialiser injection: how do you decide?

SwiftUI decides whether a view is the same view across updates using *identity*. Structural identity is the view's position and type in the hierarchy. Explicit identity comes from `ForEach` ids or `.id(_:)`. Identity controls how long `@State` lives and when transitions run.
An `if`/`else` with two different views creates two identities. Toggling destroys one view's state. A single view with a conditional modifier keeps it.
Pitfalls

items: Using `.id(UUID())` in `body`. Every render becomes a new view and state is lost constantly.
Wrapping branches in `AnyView` to make them the same type. Identity is still lost, and diffing gets worse.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: Explain structural vs explicit identity and a bug each one can cause.

Before iOS 17, a model class conformed to `ObservableObject` and marked properties `@Published`. The view that created it used `@StateObject`, others used `@ObservedObject`, and deep views used `@EnvironmentObject`. Any published change invalidated every observing view.

Migration is mechanical. Replace `ObservableObject` and `@Published` with `@Observable`. `@StateObject` becomes `@State`, `@ObservedObject` becomes a plain property (or `@Bindable` when you need `$` bindings), and `@EnvironmentObject` becomes `@Environment(Type.self)`. Unlike `@StateObject`, `@State` evaluates its initial value each time the view's init runs, keeping only the first. Keep that init cheap. To support iOS 16 as well, keep `ObservableObject` or use Point-Free's swift-perception backport.
Pitfalls

items: Mixing `@Published` into an `@Observable` class. The macro already tracks the properties.
Doing network work in the model's `init` under `@State`. It can run on every parent re-render.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: What changes in rendering behaviour when you migrate to @Observable?

modules.title: Layout, Lists & Custom Layout
modules.summary: Lists, lazy stacks, grids, geometry and writing your own Layout.

blocks.text: `List` gives you platform styling, cell reuse, swipe actions, selection and pull-to-refresh. `LazyVStack` inside a `ScrollView` gives a custom look but builds rows lazily without recycling them.
Rows need stable identity so inserts, deletes and animations target the right row.
Pitfalls

items: `ForEach(orders.indices)` with bindings. Deleting a row can crash on a stale index.
Putting a `List` inside a `ScrollView`. Both try to scroll.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: When do you choose `List` over `LazyVStack`?

links.title: Stacks, Grids, and Outlines in SwiftUI

blocks.text: `LazyVGrid` builds cells as they scroll in. Its columns are `.fixed`, `.flexible` or `.adaptive(minimum:)`, which fits as many columns as the width allows, so one grid works on iPhone and iPad. `Grid` is eager and aligns real rows and columns, which suits spec tables and forms, not long feeds.
`ViewThatFits` tries its children in order and shows the first that fits. Two buttons side by side become a stack on a narrow phone or at large text sizes, with no size-class code.
Pitfalls

items: `Grid` with hundreds of rows. It builds them all up front.
Fixed column counts that look sparse on iPad and cramped on an iPhone SE.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: Grid vs LazyVGrid: when do you use each?

links.title: Stacks, Grids, and Outlines in SwiftUI

blocks.text: `GeometryReader` takes all the space it's offered, places its content at the top-leading corner, and reports its size and frame. That makes it easy to break layouts with, so keep it for drawing that truly depends on size.

Newer tools cover most of its old uses. `containerRelativeFrame` sizes a view relative to its scroll container. `onGeometryChange` reports a size change without wrapping your layout. `visualEffect` applies scroll-position effects without writing to `@State` on every frame.
Pitfalls

items: A `GeometryReader` in every list row. It's greedy and adds layout passes.
Writing geometry into `@State` that changes the same geometry, which creates an update loop.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: Why is GeometryReader called greedy, and what do you use instead?

When stacks and grids can't express a layout, such as tag chips that wrap onto new lines, write your own. A `Layout` answers two questions. `sizeThatFits` asks how big you'd like to be for a given proposal. `placeSubviews` asks where each child goes inside the bounds.
Each child is measured by asking for its ideal size (`.unspecified`) and then placed with an explicit proposal.
Pitfalls

items: Forgetting that `proposal.width` can be nil (an ideal-size query).
Measuring expensive subviews twice. Use the `cache` parameter for heavy layouts.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: Why would you write a custom `Layout` instead of using `GeometryReader`?

iOS 17 made scroll views controllable. `scrollTargetBehavior(.paging)` or `.viewAligned` snaps content into place. `scrollPosition(id:)` reads and sets which item is visible. `scrollTransition` styles items as they move in and out. Mark the container with `scrollTargetLayout()` so these APIs know what the items are.

`ScrollViewReader` still works for jumping to an id, such as a “Top” button. For endless feeds, trigger the next page from rows near the end (Module 13, lesson 6). iOS 18 adds `onScrollGeometryChange` for reacting to the offset.
Pitfalls

items: `scrollPosition(id:)` without `scrollTargetLayout()`. The position never updates.
Passing an optional id to `scrollTo`. It compares `Optional(id)` with the row ids and never matches.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: How would you build a full-screen story pager with a page indicator?

modules.title: Navigation & App Structure
modules.summary: Value-based NavigationStack, a router object, deep links, sheets and app lifecycle.

blocks.text: Since iOS 16, navigation is data. Push a `Hashable` value onto a path and a matching `navigationDestination` decides what to show. Keeping the path in an `@Observable` router means any screen can navigate without knowing the destination's view type, and the stack becomes testable.
Model routes as an enum so the compiler makes sure every destination is handled.
Pitfalls

items: Placing `navigationDestination` inside a lazy container such as a `List` row. It may not be registered when you push.
Mixing `NavigationLink(destination:)` with path-based navigation. The path then won't reflect what's on screen.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: How would you pop to root from a deeply nested screen?

A deep link is a URL translated into navigation state. Parse it into your `Route` enum in one place, the router, and every entry point (custom scheme, universal link, push notification tap, Live Activity tap) can reuse that one function.
Reset the stack before pushing so a link always lands on a predictable screen.

diagram.title: flowchart
diagram.caption: Custom schemes, universal links, notification taps and Live Activity taps all end at one parser, so they behave the same. Unknown links are ignored rather than crashing or opening a blank screen.

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Handling links inside a child view that may not exist yet when the app launches cold.
Trusting the URL. Validate ids before you hit the network.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: How do you route a push notification tap to a specific order screen?

lessons.title: Sheets, covers and alerts driven by items

blocks.text: Presentation is state. `sheet(item:)` shows a sheet for one Identifiable value and dismisses when that value becomes nil, so the sheet can never show stale data. Use `presentationDetents` for half-height sheets, and `interactiveDismissDisabled` when a swipe would throw away unsaved edits.
Model errors as a `LocalizedError` enum and pass it to `alert(isPresented:error:)`. The alert's title and message then come from the error itself. Destructive actions go in a `confirmationDialog`.
Pitfalls

items: A Bool sheet plus a separate selected item. The sheet can open before the selection is set, or show the previous item.
Stacking two `.sheet` modifiers on one view for two different flows. Use one item enum instead.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: Why prefer sheet(item:) over sheet(isPresented:)?

The `@main App` struct declares scenes, and a `WindowGroup` is your app's window. App-delegate work such as receiving the push token still goes through `@UIApplicationDelegateAdaptor`. React to `scenePhase` to refresh stale data on foreground and save drafts on background.

Give each tab its own `NavigationStack`, so switching tabs keeps each one's position. Bind the selection to an enum so you can switch tabs from code, such as a push opening Orders. `@SceneStorage` restores the selected tab after the system relaunches your app.
Pitfalls

items: One `NavigationStack` wrapped around the whole `TabView`. Pushes then cover the tab bar, and tabs share one history.
Heavy work in `App.init`. It delays the first frame. Start it in `.task` after launch.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: Where does push-token registration live in a SwiftUI app?
