modules.title: Animation & Gestures
modules.summary: Implicit and explicit animation, transitions, springs, gestures and Reduce Motion.

lessons.title: Implicit vs explicit animation and transitions

blocks.text: `withAnimation` animates every view that depends on the state you change inside it. `.animation(_:value:)` animates one subtree whenever a specific value changes. Transitions describe how a view *enters and leaves*, so they only run when the view is inserted or removed inside an animated change.
Springs are the default in modern SwiftUI. They keep their velocity when interrupted, which makes rapid taps feel natural.
Pitfalls

items: Calling `.animation(.default)` without a `value:`. It's deprecated and animates far more than you meant.
A transition that never plays because the view was replaced (new identity) rather than inserted.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: Why might a transition not animate, and how do you fix it?

lessons.title: Gestures: drag, long press and composition

blocks.text: `DragGesture` reports translation as the finger moves. Store the in-flight value in `@GestureState`, which resets automatically when the finger lifts, so a released knob springs back with no cleanup code. Decide the outcome in `onEnded`, and use a threshold so the user doesn't have to drag to the exact end.

Compose gestures with `sequenced(before:)` (hold, then drag), `simultaneousGesture` (double-tap to like while scrolling) and `highPriorityGesture`. Every custom gesture needs an accessibility action, because VoiceOver users can't drag.
Pitfalls

items: A `DragGesture` inside a `ScrollView` that steals scrolling. Give it a `minimumDistance` or restrict it to one axis.
Gesture-only actions with no accessibility alternative.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: How would you build a swipe-to-confirm control that's safe and accessible?

`matchedGeometryEffect` links two views with the same id in a namespace. When one is removed and the other inserted inside an animation, SwiftUI animates the frame between them, which is how a sliding tab underline works. It works within one view hierarchy, not across a navigation push.

For pushes, iOS 18 adds the zoom transition. Mark the tapped poster with `matchedTransitionSource(id:in:)` and the destination with `navigationTransition(.zoom(sourceID:in:))`. The detail screen grows out of the poster, and the user can drag it back interactively.
Pitfalls

items: Two views with the same matched id visible at the same time. SwiftUI warns, and the animation jumps.
Changing the selection without `withAnimation`. The views match, but nothing animates.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: How would you animate a poster into its detail screen?

`phaseAnimator` cycles through a list of phases and animates between them, which suits a pulsing “connecting” dot, with no timers or `onAppear` loops. `keyframeAnimator` drives several properties along separate tracks with their own timing and curves: a payment check that pops, overshoots, tilts and settles.
Keyframes are for fixed sequences. For UI that follows state, keep using `withAnimation`. Respect Reduce Motion by swapping big motion for a fade.
Pitfalls

items: Driving state-dependent UI with keyframes. They play a fixed script and ignore changes made mid-way.
Infinite phase animations left running off-screen in long lists.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: When do you reach for keyframes instead of withAnimation?

modules.title: MVVM & Clean Architecture
modules.summary: @Observable view models, screen state as enums, dependency injection and clean layering.

blocks.text: The view model owns presentation state and the logic that changes it. The view only renders that state and forwards user intent. Model the screen's state as an enum so impossible combinations, such as loading and failed at once, can't exist, and the view's `switch` covers every case.
Mark view models `@MainActor`: they drive UI, so every mutation happens on the main thread and the compiler checks it.
Pitfalls

items: View models that import SwiftUI and return `Color`s or `View`s. Keep them UI-framework-free where you can.
One giant view model per tab. Split by screen, and share state through models or services.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: How do you make this view model unit-testable?

Inject dependencies through initialisers, behind protocols, and wire the real ones once at the app root. Previews and tests pass fakes. No singletons leak into business logic, and every dependency is visible in the init signature.
This is the same pattern as the `AppEnvironment` container in your bbInstant rebuild.
Pitfalls

items: A service locator that you call from inside a view model. Dependencies become invisible again.
Injecting a 30-property container into every screen. Pass only what the screen uses.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: Compare constructor injection with environment injection in SwiftUI.

lessons.title: Clean layers: View → ViewModel → UseCase → Repository

blocks.text: Clean layering has one rule: dependencies point inward. The domain layer (entities, use cases, repository protocols) is plain Swift with no SwiftUI, URLSession or SwiftData. The data layer implements those protocols and maps API DTOs into domain types, so a renamed JSON field changes one mapper instead of fifty views. Presentation depends only on the domain.

A use case earns its place when it holds a business rule, such as hiding test orders or sorting by value. One that only forwards a repository call is ceremony, so skip it. In `BBI_SWIFTUI_APP`, `Core/Networking` and `Core/Storage` hold the data layer's tools, and each folder under `Features/` holds a feature's views, view models and models.

diagram.title: architecture
diagram.caption: Arrows point inward: presentation knows the domain, and the data layer implements a protocol the domain owns. The domain never imports SwiftUI, URLSession or SwiftData, so an API change stays in the data layer.

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: DTOs with snake_case fields reaching views. Every API change then ripples through the UI.
A use case per CRUD call that adds nothing. More files without more clarity.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: Walk through the layers of a feature and where each kind of code lives.

lessons.title: MVC, MVVM, VIPER and TCA compared

blocks.text: They differ in where state, logic and navigation live. **MVC** on iOS puts all three in the view controller, which grows huge. **MVVM** moves state and logic into a view model that the view binds to. **VIPER** splits a screen into View, Interactor, Presenter, Entity and Router, with protocols between each: very testable, but heavy on files. **TCA** (The Composable Architecture, from Point-Free) uses State, Action, Reducer and Store with explicit dependencies, a unidirectional flow and exhaustive tests, in exchange for a library dependency and a learning curve.

In an interview, choose by context, not fashion. Most SwiftUI teams use MVVM with `@Observable` view models and a router. A reducer pays off where many events interleave, such as players, chat and checkout. VIPER fits large UIKit codebases with strict module boundaries. Show you know the trade-off: more structure buys testability and consistency at the cost of ceremony.
Pitfalls

items: Choosing VIPER for a five-screen app. The ceremony outweighs the benefit.
Calling it MVVM while the view model is a massive view controller with a new name. Keep view models screen-sized.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: Which architecture would you choose for a new SwiftUI app with six engineers, and why?

lessons.title: Modularising features with Swift Package Manager

blocks.text: Local Swift packages turn folder conventions into rules the compiler enforces. A feature package can import `Networking` and `DesignSystem` but not another feature, so accidental coupling becomes a build error. Each package builds, tests and previews on its own, which is much faster than the full app.
Access control becomes architecture. Only a feature's entry point is `public`, and its subviews, view models and mappers stay `internal`. The app target wires features together at the root.
Pitfalls

items: Marking everything `public` to make a build error go away. The boundary then means nothing.
Features importing each other. Move what they share into a lower-level package.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: How would you split a large app into modules, and what do you gain?

modules.title: Design Patterns in Swift
modules.summary: Creational, structural and behavioural patterns as they actually appear in iOS code.

blocks.text: A singleton is one shared instance with a private init. It suits truly app-wide services such as analytics or logging. The cost is hidden global state that tests can't replace. The fix: conform it to a protocol and inject the protocol.
A factory centralises the decision of *which* concrete type to build, so feature flags and A/B tests live in one place.
Pitfalls

items: Singletons that hold mutable user state. Logout then leaves stale data behind.
Builders for objects that default parameter values already handle.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: What's wrong with singletons, and how do you keep one testable?

An adapter wraps a third-party SDK behind your own protocol. Your app depends on the protocol, and swapping payment vendors touches one file. A decorator wraps an object that conforms to the same protocol to add behaviour such as logging, caching or auth without changing it.
Here the adapter also bridges a callback API into `async` with a checked continuation.
Pitfalls

items: Resuming a continuation twice, or never. The first crashes, the second hangs the task forever.
Leaking SDK types (their result enums) through your protocol. Map them to your own types.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: How would you make a vendor payment SDK swappable and testable?

Strategy puts interchangeable algorithms behind one protocol: discount rules, sort orders, retry policies. The State pattern in Swift is usually an enum plus a transition function. Illegal states can't be expressed, and illegal transitions are ignored in one visible place.
A vending machine door is a real state machine. Model it this way and the socket and BLE layers can only send events.

diagram.title: state machine
diagram.caption: Each state accepts exactly one event. Anything else, such as a second unlock tap while unlocking, leaves the state unchanged and gets logged, so the socket and Bluetooth layers can't put the door into an impossible state.

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Booleans like `isUnlocking`, `isOpen` and `isClosing` that can all be true at once.
Silently ignoring unexpected events with no logging. Log them, because they reveal protocol bugs.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: Model a payment flow as a state machine. Which transitions are illegal?

Put navigation decisions behind a small protocol so they're testable without views. A coordinator decides what happens next, such as showing a receipt or retrying payment, and a fake router in tests records the calls. In SwiftUI the concrete router usually mutates a `NavigationPath` (Module 7).
A repository hides where data comes from. A common shape returns an async stream that yields cached data immediately and then fresh data from the network, so the screen is instant and still correct.
Pitfalls

items: Coordinators that build and hold views. Keep them to decisions, and let the router own presentation.
Repositories exposing cache policy to callers. The caller should only ask for orders.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: How do you test navigation logic without launching the UI?

lessons.title: Delegation and Observer in Apple frameworks

blocks.text: Delegation hands decisions or events to one object through a protocol. The delegate reference is `weak`, and the protocol is limited to `AnyObject`. Core Bluetooth, CLLocationManager and AVFoundation still talk this way. Wrap them once in an `AsyncStream` so the rest of the app writes `for await`.

Observer comes in several forms, from loosest to tightest coupling: NotificationCenter (app-wide broadcasts), KVO (Objective-C properties such as `AVPlayer.timeControlStatus`), Combine publishers and Observation. Pick the narrowest one that reaches every listener.
Pitfalls

items: A strong delegate reference. The two objects keep each other alive.
Leaving the stream open when Bluetooth is off. The UI waits forever instead of explaining.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: How would you expose a delegate-based SDK to SwiftUI code?

modules.title: GCD & OperationQueue
modules.summary: Dispatch queues, QoS, groups, barriers, semaphores, deadlocks and thread safety.

blocks.text: GCD runs closures on queues backed by a system thread pool. A serial queue runs one task at a time in order. A concurrent queue may run many. `async` returns immediately. `sync` blocks the caller until the work finishes.
UI work belongs on `DispatchQueue.main`. Calling `sync` onto the queue you're already running on deadlocks, because the queue waits for itself.
Pitfalls

items: Using `.userInteractive` for everything. QoS is a promise to the scheduler, so keep it honest.
Assuming a global concurrent queue preserves order. It doesn't.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: Explain how `DispatchQueue.main.sync` called from the main thread deadlocks.
A `DispatchGroup` waits for several callbacks and then continues once. A barrier block on a *custom* concurrent queue gives you a reader-writer lock: reads run in parallel and a write runs alone.
Semaphores block threads. That causes priority inversion and, inside Swift Concurrency, can starve the cooperative pool. Treat them as legacy.
Pitfalls

items: Barriers on global queues do nothing. They only work on queues you create.
An unbalanced `enter`/`leave`. Extra leaves crash, and missing ones mean `notify` never fires.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: Build a thread-safe cache two ways: GCD barrier and actor.

`OperationQueue` runs `Operation` objects with three things GCD lacks: dependencies between operations, a concurrency limit, and cancellation state you can check. Exporting receipts (fetch, then render the PDF, then upload) is a small dependency graph instead of nested callbacks.

Cancellation is cooperative: `cancelAllOperations()` only sets `isCancelled`, and your code has to check it. Asynchronous operations need a subclass that manages `isExecuting` and `isFinished` through KVO, which is error-prone. In new code, a task group with limited concurrency usually replaces this, but you'll meet OperationQueue in older codebases.
Pitfalls

items: Blocking inside `main()` while waiting for an async callback with a semaphore.
Long loops that never check `isCancelled`.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: When would you still choose OperationQueue over a TaskGroup?

When state must be shared synchronously, without `await`, use a lock. `Mutex` and `Atomic` from the Synchronization module (iOS 18) are the modern choice. On older systems, `OSAllocatedUnfairLock` (iOS 16) wraps its state the same way. All of them hold the lock only for the duration of a closure, so you can't forget to unlock.

Locks fix data races, where two threads touch memory at once. They don't fix race conditions, where logic depends on timing. Checking “is it missing?” and then “add it” in two separate locked calls still lets another thread slip in between. Do the whole decision inside one critical section.
Pitfalls

items: Trying to hold a lock across `await`. You can't, and you shouldn't. Use an actor for async state.
Calling slow work such as network or disk inside `withLock`. Every other thread waits.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: What's the difference between a data race and a race condition?

links.title: Eliminate data races using Swift Concurrency

blocks.text: Migrate in small steps that each ship. First wrap callback APIs with continuations so callers can move to `await` while the implementation stays the same. Xcode's Refactor menu can add async wrappers for you. Then replace serial queues that protect state with actors, and `DispatchGroup` fan-outs with task groups.

The rule that changes is “never block”. Swift Concurrency runs on a pool with roughly one thread per core. A `semaphore.wait()` or synchronous network call inside async code starves that pool. GCD would spawn more threads (thread explosion), but the cooperative pool doesn't, so the app hangs.
Pitfalls

items: `DispatchSemaphore.wait()` inside async code. It blocks a cooperative thread and can deadlock the pool.
Leaving `DispatchQueue.main.async` inside `@MainActor` code. It's redundant and reorders work.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: How would you migrate a large GCD codebase without a big-bang rewrite?

modules.title: Swift Concurrency
modules.summary: async/await, structured concurrency, actors, MainActor, Sendable, AsyncStream and Swift 6.

blocks.text: An `async` function can suspend at each `await` without blocking a thread. Code reads top to bottom, errors propagate with `try`, and the compiler won't let you forget a callback.
In SwiftUI, start work with `.task(id:)`. It starts when the view appears and is cancelled automatically when the view disappears or the id changes.
Pitfalls

items: Wrapping everything in `Task { }` inside button actions and never cancelling it.
`Task.detached` to “get off the main thread”. You lose priority and task-locals. Use a nonisolated or `@concurrent` function instead.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: What does `.task(id:)` do that `onAppear { Task { } }` doesn't?

lessons.title: Structured concurrency: async let and TaskGroup

blocks.text: Child tasks are bound to their parent's scope. The parent can't return until its children finish. If one child throws, its siblings are cancelled. Cancelling the parent cancels every child. Nothing leaks.
Use `async let` for a fixed, small set of concurrent calls, such as a home screen's three requests. Use a task group when the count is dynamic.

diagram.title: task tree
diagram.caption: The three requests run at the same time, and the parent can't return until all of them finish. If `banners()` throws, the other two are cancelled automatically and the error comes out of the parent's `await`.

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Adding 5,000 tasks at once to a group. Limit concurrency by adding the next task as each one finishes.
Mutating a shared array from inside `addTask`. Collect results through the group instead.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: Compare `async let` and `withTaskGroup`. What happens to siblings when one fails?

An actor protects its mutable state by running one piece of its code at a time. Callers outside must `await`. Actors are *reentrant*: while one call is suspended at an `await`, another call can run, so state may change across a suspension point.
Token refresh shows this. Without the stored `refreshTask`, five concurrent 401s would trigger five refreshes. With it, the later callers join the request already in flight.

diagram.title: flowchart
diagram.caption: The `await` in the highlighted box is a suspension point. Other callers can enter the actor there, which is reentrancy, and they find the stored task and join it instead of starting a second refresh.

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Assuming state checked before an `await` is still true after it.
Silencing Sendable warnings with `@unchecked Sendable` on types that really are unsafe.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: What is actor reentrancy? Show a bug it causes and how you fix it.

links.title: Protect mutable state with Swift actors
Eliminate data races using Swift Concurrency

blocks.text: Cancellation is cooperative. A task is only *asked* to stop. `URLSession` and `Task.sleep` check for you and throw `CancellationError`. Long loops must check `Task.isCancelled` themselves.

`AsyncStream` turns a callback or delegate source, such as a socket, BLE notifications or location, into a `for await` loop. Clean up in `onTermination`, which runs when the consumer's task is cancelled.
Pitfalls

items: Unbounded buffering for a chatty socket, which grows memory without limit.
Swallowing `CancellationError` and showing “Something went wrong” to a user who just navigated away.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: How do you bridge a delegate-based API into async/await?

Swift 6 language mode turns data-race diagnostics into compile errors. You switch it on *per target*, so migrate in stages. First set `SWIFT_STRICT_CONCURRENCY = complete` while staying in Swift 5 mode, and fix the warnings. Then set `SWIFT_VERSION = 6`. Start with leaf modules (`Core`, models, networking), then features, and the app target last.

Most errors fall into four shapes: global mutable state, a non-Sendable type crossing an actor boundary, UI code called from a nonisolated context, and callbacks from SDKs that predate concurrency. The fixes are almost always value-type models that are `Sendable`, `@MainActor` on UI-facing types, an `actor` for shared mutable state, and `@preconcurrency import` for unannotated SDKs.

Swift 6.2 (Xcode 26) adds approachable concurrency. App targets can set **Default Actor Isolation** to `MainActor`, so unannotated code runs on the main actor. `nonisolated async` functions run on the caller's actor, and `@concurrent` explicitly moves work onto the concurrent pool. Use main-actor-by-default for app targets, and keep shared libraries nonisolated.
Pitfalls

items: Silencing errors with `@unchecked Sendable` or `nonisolated(unsafe)`. The race doesn't go away; it moves to runtime. Leave a comment saying what guarantees safety, or don't use them.
Flipping the app target to Swift 6 first. You then get hundreds of errors from dependencies you haven't migrated. Go leaf modules first.
Making every service `@MainActor` to make the errors stop. Decoding and image work then runs on the main thread. Mark it `@concurrent` or move it to an actor.
Turning on default MainActor isolation in a shared package. Every caller then has to hop to the main actor. Use it only for app and UI targets.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: How would you migrate a 200k-line app to Swift 6 language mode without freezing feature work?

links.title: Eliminate data races using Swift Concurrency

blocks.text: A continuation suspends an async function until a callback hands back the result. `withCheckedContinuation` catches misuse: resuming twice traps, and never resuming logs a leak warning. `withUnsafeContinuation` skips the checks for a tiny saving. Use checked unless profiling proves otherwise.

Every path must resume exactly once, including errors, timeouts and early returns. Cancelling the task doesn't resume a continuation, so wrap it in `withTaskCancellationHandler` and tell the underlying SDK to stop. The SDK's callback then resumes it with an error.
Pitfalls

items: Calling `currentState()` twice before the first answer. The second call overwrites the stored continuation, and the first one leaks. Reject or queue concurrent calls.
A callback that may fire more than once, such as progress updates. Use an `AsyncStream` instead.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: What goes wrong if a continuation is resumed twice or never?

modules.title: Networking & API Layer
modules.summary: A typed Endpoint + APIClient, Codable in depth, auth refresh, retries and real-time sockets.

blocks.text: A good network layer has three parts. An `Endpoint` value describes a request and the type it returns. An `APIClient` protocol sends any endpoint. An error enum separates transport, HTTP, auth and decoding failures so the UI can react to each one.
Because the client is a protocol, you can decorate it (auth, logging, retry) and fake it in tests. Feature code only ever writes `try await client.send(.products(machineID:))`.

diagram.title: request lifecycle
diagram.caption: Feature code only ever calls `send(.endpoint)`. The authenticated wrapper adds the token, and on a 401 it refreshes once and retries once. Other non-2xx responses and decoding failures become typed `APIError` cases instead of crashes.

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: One giant `NetworkManager` singleton with a method per API. It can't be faked, decorated or split.
Throwing raw `DecodingError`s at the UI. Map them to user-facing messages at the view model.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: Design a network layer for a new app. What are the pieces, and how do you test it?

lessons.title: Codable in depth: keys, custom decoding and dates

blocks.text: Real APIs rarely match Swift naming. Prices may arrive as strings, keys may be missing, and dates come in several formats. `CodingKeys` handles renames. A custom `init(from:)` handles everything else, and a bad payload still produces a precise `DecodingError` you can log.
Decide on purpose what “missing” means for each field: an optional, a default value, or a hard failure.
Pitfalls

items: `keyDecodingStrategy = .convertFromSnakeCase` combined with custom `CodingKeys`. The strategy converts keys first, so your snake_case raw values never match.
Decoding `Decimal` straight from a JSON number. It passes through `Double` and can lose precision.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: How do you decode a field that is sometimes a string and sometimes a number?

Auth is a decorator over the plain client. It attaches the token, and on a 401 it invalidates the token, refreshes once and retries once. The single-flight `TokenRefresher` actor from Module 12 makes sure concurrent 401s share one refresh.
Retry only transient transport failures. Use exponential backoff, cap the attempts, and let cancellation stop the wait.

diagram.title: flowchart
diagram.caption: Only transient transport errors are retried, never a 401 or a payment POST without an idempotency key. The delay doubles each time, and because it's `Task.sleep`, leaving the screen cancels the wait.

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Retrying a non-idempotent POST such as a payment. Use an idempotency key, or don't retry.
Logging the user out on any refresh error. Distinguish “refresh token expired” from “offline”.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: Five requests get a 401 at the same moment. Walk through what your client does.

links.title: Protect mutable state with Swift actors

blocks.text: Use caches in layers. `URLCache` honours `Cache-Control` for fairly static data such as catalogue pages and banners. Conditional requests save bandwidth: send the last `ETag` in `If-None-Match`, and a `304 Not Modified` reply means what you have is still current. On top of that, keep a persistent copy (SwiftData or files) so the app opens with data even offline.

Stale-while-revalidate is the pattern users feel. Show the cached copy instantly with a “Updated 5 min ago” label, refresh in the background, and replace it when the fresh data arrives. Invalidate the cache whenever your own mutations change the data.

diagram.title: data flow
diagram.caption: The screen gets the cached list immediately, so it opens instantly and works offline. Revalidation sends the last ETag: a `304` means the cache is current and nothing is downloaded, and a `200` replaces it.

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Personalised responses, such as a wallet balance, in a shared URL cache. Mark them `no-store` or keep them out.
Showing cached prices at checkout without revalidating.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: Design offline support for an order history screen.

`URLSessionWebSocketTask` gives you `send` and an async `receive()` that returns one frame at a time. The hard part isn't sending frames. It's keeping a session alive on a phone: networks switch, the app gets suspended, and a connection can go half-open, where nothing arrives but no error is thrown either.

A robust client has four parts. A **supervisor loop** owns the whole lifecycle: connect, run, back off, reconnect. While one connection is live, a **task group** runs the receive loop and the heartbeat side by side, so the first failure tears both down. **Stale detection** compares the time of the last received frame to a deadline instead of trusting the socket to report errors. One **`AsyncStream`** is created up front and every event flows through it.

Back off exponentially *with jitter*. Otherwise every vending machine's users reconnect in the same second after a server restart. Reset the failure count only when the server confirms auth, not when the TCP connection opens. When the app goes to the background, iOS suspends the socket. Stop the session on `scenePhase == .background` and start a fresh one on `.active`.

diagram.title: state machine
diagram.caption: The session is *live* only after the server confirms auth, which is also when the failure count resets. A receive error or 45 s of silence moves to *waiting*, which backs off with jitter and reconnects. Calling `stop()` works from any state.

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Creating a new `AsyncStream` each time someone reads a `messages` property. Each one replaces the last continuation, so earlier subscribers go silent. An AsyncStream has one consumer, so fan events out from a model if several screens need them.
Reconnect logic that runs inside the task it cancels. The next `Task.sleep` throws immediately, and the retry loop quietly gives up.
Resetting the backoff when the socket opens instead of when auth succeeds. A server that accepts and then rejects you gets hammered every 2 seconds.
Sending heartbeats without checking that anything comes back. A half-open connection can leave `receive()` waiting forever.
Building JSON with string interpolation. A token containing a quote breaks the frame. Encode a struct instead.

blocks.text: In the capstone

Found by reading `Integrations/Machine/Socket/MachineSocket.swift`, then fixed in the repo on 3 Nov 2026. Each fix type-checks in Swift 5 strict-concurrency and Swift 6 mode, and a wire-format check confirmed outgoing messages are unchanged. Not yet tested on a device.

items: **Fixed · single stream.** Before: every read of `messages` built a new stream and replaced the stored continuation, so earlier listeners went silent. After: one stream is created in `init` with `AsyncStream.makeStream(bufferingPolicy: .bufferingNewest(100))`, so events that arrive before the listener starts are buffered.

**Fixed · reconnect cancelled itself.** Before: `attemptReconnect()` ran inside `listenTask` and called `disconnect()`, which cancelled that task, so it stopped after one try and the delay stayed at 2 s. After: `scheduleReconnect()` runs each attempt in its own `reconnectTask`, `closeSocket()` tears down only the connection, the delay grows 2, 4, 8, 16, 30 s, the count resets only on `auth_success`, and the state becomes `.failed` after 5 attempts.

**Fixed · half-open connections.** Before: heartbeats were sent but nothing checked that anything came back. After: every received frame stamps `lastMessageAt`. If 45 s (three heartbeat intervals) pass without a frame, the heartbeat closes the socket and schedules a reconnect.

**Fixed · hand-built JSON.** Before: the token was interpolated into a string literal, so a quote broke the frame. After: an `Encodable` payload goes through `JSONEncoder` (slashes left unescaped). It's the same JSON object, though key order can differ.

**Fixed · money as Double.** `transactionComplete(totalAmount:)` is now `Decimal`, read from the number's string form, and amounts sent as strings now parse instead of silently becoming 0. `OrderSummaryView` and `LocalStore` still use `Double`; that's a separate follow-up.

**Still open.** The heartbeat starts only after authentication succeeds, so a server that accepts the connection but never answers `auth` can still leave the socket waiting. An auth timeout would close that gap.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: Design a real-time client for a vending machine session. How do you detect a dead connection and avoid a reconnect storm?

links.title: Protect mutable state with Swift actors

blocks.text: Offset pagination (`?page=3`) skips or repeats items when new posts arrive while the user scrolls. Cursor pagination (`?after=abc`) resumes from a stable marker. Request the next page a few rows before the end, allow only one load at a time, and drop duplicate ids (the FeedPager in the video-platform case study).

Image cells should cancel their work when they scroll away, which `.task(id:)` does for free. They also share one pipeline actor that caches, de-duplicates and downsamples. The pipeline's own download continues even if one cell cancels, because another cell may still want that image.
Pitfalls

items: `AsyncImage` in a long feed. It has no in-memory cache and reloads as rows reappear.
Caching full-resolution `UIImage`s. Cache the downsampled versions with a cost limit.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: Offset vs cursor pagination: which, and why?

modules.title: Persistence
modules.summary: UserDefaults, Keychain, SwiftData, Core Data and the file system: what goes where.

lessons.title: Choosing storage: defaults, Keychain and files

blocks.text: Small preferences go in `UserDefaults`, through `@AppStorage` in SwiftUI. Secrets such as tokens, PINs and payment references go in the Keychain, which is encrypted and survives reinstall depending on its accessibility class. Structured app data goes in SwiftData or Core Data. Large blobs go in files: Caches if they can be re-created, Application Support if not.
The Keychain API is C-style dictionaries and `OSStatus` codes, so wrap it once.
Pitfalls

items: Auth tokens in `UserDefaults`. They're readable from an unencrypted backup.
Writing large JSON to `UserDefaults`. It's loaded into memory at launch.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: Where do you store an access token, a feature flag cache, and 200 MB of images?

`@Model` turns a class into a persisted entity. `@Query` fetches and keeps a SwiftUI view in sync automatically. Attach a `ModelContainer` at the scene and read the `ModelContext` from the environment to insert and delete.
Use it as a cache for orders and receipts so history opens instantly and works offline.
Pitfalls

items: Passing `@Model` objects across actors. Pass the `persistentModelID` and re-fetch.
Heavy imports on the main context. Use a `@ModelActor` for background work.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: SwiftData or Core Data for a new app targeting iOS 17+? Justify it.

`NSPersistentContainer` owns the store. Its `viewContext` runs on the main queue for the UI, and background contexts do imports. Every managed object belongs to its context's queue, so touch it only inside `perform`, and pass `NSManagedObjectID`s between contexts, never objects. For tens of thousands of rows, `NSBatchInsertRequest` writes straight to the store.

Additive changes, such as a new optional attribute, migrate automatically (lightweight migration). Bigger changes need staged migrations. In SwiftData you describe each version as a `VersionedSchema` and the steps between them in a `SchemaMigrationPlan`.
Pitfalls

items: Passing an `NSManagedObject` to another thread. It crashes intermittently. Pass its `objectID`.
Running batch inserts and wondering why the list doesn't update. They skip the context, so merge the object IDs as shown, or use persistent history tracking.
Calling `fatalError` when the store fails to load. A failed migration then crashes the app on every launch.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: How do you import 50,000 records without freezing the UI?

Each container directory has a meaning. Documents holds user-created data and is backed up. Application Support holds app data the user doesn't manage, and you have to create it first. Caches holds anything you can re-create, and the system may purge it. tmp is for short-lived files you delete yourself. Putting a 300 MB catalogue cache in Documents bloats iCloud backups and can draw App Review attention.

Write sensitive files with a data-protection class, and mark re-downloadable files as excluded from backup. Large downloads use a background `URLSession`, which keeps going after the app is suspended. Move the file inside `didFinishDownloadingTo`, because the system deletes it when that method returns.
Pitfalls

items: Caches in Documents. They're backed up and visible, and Review may flag them.
Reading the downloaded file asynchronously after `didFinishDownloadingTo` returns. By then it's gone.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: Where do you store receipts, a re-downloadable catalogue, and a draft cart?

modules.title: Combine & Reactive Streams
modules.summary: Publishers and operators, and when async sequences or Observation replace them.

blocks.text: Combine models values over time. A publisher emits, operators transform, a subscriber receives. Debounced search is the canonical example: wait for typing to pause, drop duplicates, cancel the stale request with `switchToLatest`, and deliver on main.
`assign(to: &$property)` ties the subscription's lifetime to the object, so there's no cancellable to store and no retain cycle.
Pitfalls

items: `sink { self.results = $0 }` stored in `self.cancellables`. That's a retain cycle.
Forgetting `receive(on:)` and publishing UI changes from a background thread.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: Explain debounce vs throttle, and what `switchToLatest` solves.

For new SwiftUI code, Observation replaces `@Published`, `async` functions replace one-shot publishers, and `AsyncSequence` covers most streams. Combine still wins for time-based operator chains and existing codebases. Know both.
The same debounced search with Swift Concurrency: `.task(id: query)` restarts on every keystroke, and the previous task's `sleep` throws when it is cancelled.
Pitfalls

items: `try?` on the sleep. Cancellation is swallowed and the stale search still runs.
Rewriting stable Combine code just to modernise it. Migrate when you touch it.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: When would you still choose Combine in 2026?

Subjects let imperative code push values into Combine. `PassthroughSubject` forwards events and keeps nothing, so a late subscriber misses earlier sends. `CurrentValueSubject` holds state and gives the latest value to every new subscriber. Expose them as `AnyPublisher` so outside code can't send.

`subscribe(on:)` moves upstream work, such as subscription and production, to a scheduler. `receive(on:)` moves delivery downstream. A plain publisher chain re-runs its work for each subscriber. `share()` runs it once for subscribers that are attached when it starts, without replaying to late ones.
Pitfalls

items: Exposing a subject publicly. Any caller can then send fake events.
Expecting `share()` to replay to a subscriber that attaches after the value arrived. It doesn't.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: PassthroughSubject or CurrentValueSubject: how do you choose?

modules.title: Testing
modules.summary: Swift Testing, protocol fakes, URLProtocol stubs, async tests and UI tests.

blocks.text: Swift Testing (Xcode 16+) uses `@Test` functions, the `#expect` and `#require` macros, parameterised arguments and struct-based suites that run in parallel by default. Failures print the actual values of the expression, not just “false”.
Because the view model takes a protocol, the test controls the service's result fully, with no network involved.
Pitfalls

items: Asserting on the loading state without controlling timing. Use fakes that suspend until you release them.
Tests that share static state while running in parallel. Mark the suite `.serialized`.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: What does Swift Testing give you over XCTest?

lessons.title: Testing the network layer with URLProtocol

blocks.text: To test the real `URLSessionAPIClient`, including request building, status mapping and decoding, without a server, register a `URLProtocol` subclass on an ephemeral session. It intercepts every request and returns whatever response you script.
Fake the `APIClient` protocol for feature tests. Use the URLProtocol stub only for the client itself.
Pitfalls

items: Registering the stub globally with `URLProtocol.registerClass`. Other tests then hit it unexpectedly.
Not asserting on the request itself: path, headers and method.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: How do you test networking code without hitting a server?

For async APIs, write `async` test methods and simply `await`. For callback APIs, create an `expectation`, fulfil it in the callback, and wait with `await fulfillment(of:timeout:)`, the async-safe replacement for `wait(for:)`.

In Swift Testing, `confirmation()` plays the same role and can require an exact count, such as “progress reported twice”. For Combine pipelines with `debounce`, inject the scheduler: a `DispatchQueue` in production and Combine's `ImmediateScheduler` in tests, so nothing waits on real time.
Pitfalls

items: Calling `wait(for:)` inside an async test. It can deadlock, so use `fulfillment(of:)`.
Generous timeouts that hide slow code. Keep them tight so regressions show up.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: How do you test a completion-handler API?

UI tests drive the real app through accessibility. Give important controls stable `accessibilityIdentifier`s instead of matching visible text, which changes with localisation. Launch with an argument such as `-uiTesting` so the app swaps in fake services. Tests then never depend on the backend, a real wallet or a real vending machine.

Snapshot tests render a view to an image and compare it with a stored reference, which catches visual regressions that unit tests miss. Point-Free's open-source swift-snapshot-testing library is the common choice. Pin the simulator, OS and locale, or snapshots fail for reasons that aren't bugs.
Pitfalls

items: `sleep(3)` before assertions. Use `waitForExistence`.
UI tests that cover every edge case. Keep them to a few critical journeys and push logic tests down to unit level.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: How do you keep UI tests fast and stable?

lessons.title: Deterministic tests: clocks, UUIDs and dates

blocks.text: Tests flake when code reads the outside world directly: `Date()`, `UUID()`, real sleeps, randomness, the network. Inject those as dependencies with production defaults, and pass fixed values in tests.

For time, depend on `any Clock<Duration>` instead of calling `Task.sleep` directly. Production passes `ContinuousClock()`, and tests pass a controllable clock, such as the TestClock in Point-Free's swift-clocks package. A 30-second OTP countdown then tests in milliseconds.
Pitfalls

items: Tests that pass only in the morning, or only in IST. Inject time zone and calendar too.
Chasing a coverage number. Coverage shows untested code, not whether the tests check anything.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: How do you test code that waits 30 seconds?

modules.title: Performance, Instruments & Debugging
modules.summary: Hangs, SwiftUI update cost, memory and the tools that measure them.

blocks.text: A hang is the main thread being too busy to respond to touches. Profile with the Time Profiler and Hangs instruments on a real device in a Release build, find the heavy main-thread frames, and move that work off the main actor.
With Swift 6.2's approachable-concurrency settings, a `nonisolated async` function runs on the caller's actor by default. Mark CPU-heavy work `@concurrent` so it really leaves the main actor.
Pitfalls

items: Profiling Debug builds on the simulator. The numbers aren't representative.
Synchronous image decoding in list cells. Downsample off the main thread.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: Users report the order history stutters. How do you investigate?

A body re-runs when something it read changes. Keep each view's dependencies narrow. Pass small value inputs to cells instead of whole models, keep identities stable, and keep formatting and sorting out of `body`.
`Self._printChanges()` (debug builds only) logs which input invalidated a view. The SwiftUI instrument shows the same data over time.
Pitfalls

items: Reading a frequently changing property (a timer, a scroll offset) high in the tree.
Leaving `_printChanges()` in shipping code.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: How do you find out why a SwiftUI view re-renders too often?

lessons.title: Memory: Allocations, Leaks and the Memory Graph

blocks.text: Run Instruments Allocations, mark a generation, repeat a flow (open and close a product, scroll a feed), and mark again. Growth that stays after each repetition is either a leak (unreachable) or abandoned memory (reachable but useless, such as an unbounded cache). The Memory Graph shows who holds it. iOS kills apps that exceed device memory limits, so this matters most on older phones.

In image-heavy apps, the biggest win is never decoding a full-size image for a thumbnail. A 4032 × 3024 photo decodes to about 48.8 MB (width × height × 4 bytes), while a 300-pt thumbnail at 3× is about 3.2 MB. Downsample with ImageIO (social case study), and keep decoded images in an `NSCache` with a cost limit so the system can evict them under pressure.
Pitfalls

items: A `[URL: UIImage]` dictionary with no limit. It grows until the app is killed.
Profiling memory on the Simulator, which has your Mac's RAM and decodes differently.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: An image feed gets killed after five minutes of scrolling. How do you investigate?

Launch time is the time before your first frame. Profile it with the App Launch template on a real device in a Release build. In `didFinishLaunching`, start only what must exist before anything else runs, such as crash reporting. Analytics, remote config, ads and warm-up work belong in a low-priority `.task` after the first frame. In production, MetricKit delivers launch histograms and hang reports from real devices.

Binary size affects download conversion and update speed. Check the App Thinning size report, remove unused assets and SDKs, prefer asset catalogs, and watch how much each dynamic framework adds to both size and launch time.
Pitfalls

items: Measuring launch in Debug builds or on the Simulator.
Deferring so much that the first tap hitches. Defer, but don't push the work onto the first interaction.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: How would you cut a 2.5-second cold launch in half?

links.title: Improve app size and runtime performance

blocks.text: A crash report tells you the exception type, the crashed thread and its backtrace. `EXC_BREAKPOINT` usually means a Swift runtime trap (force-unwrapping nil, array out of bounds, a failed precondition). `EXC_BAD_ACCESS` means invalid memory. Turning addresses into function names and line numbers needs the dSYM whose UUID matches the build. Xcode Organizer does this for TestFlight and App Store crashes, and third-party crash tools need the dSYMs uploaded.

At a breakpoint, `v` reads variables without running code, `po` evaluates expressions (and can have side effects), and `bt` prints the backtrace. Conditional breakpoints and watchpoints find “who changed this?” bugs. `Logger` from OSLog leaves privacy-aware breadcrumbs you can read in Console.
Pitfalls

items: Losing the dSYMs for a shipped build. Its crashes stay as raw addresses forever.
Using `po` on something with side effects and changing the bug while you watch it.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: Walk through diagnosing a crash that only happens in production.

links.title: Run, Break, Inspect: Explore effective debugging in LLDB
Diagnosing issues using crash reports and device logs

modules.title: Platform Integration & Shipping
modules.summary: UIKit interop, widgets and Live Activities, accessibility, signing and release.

blocks.text: `UIViewRepresentable` brings a UIKit view into SwiftUI. Make it once, update it whenever SwiftUI state changes, and use a `Coordinator` for delegates. `UIHostingController` goes the other way and is how you migrate a UIKit app screen by screen.
Your bbInstant migration replaced the UIKit app in one clean-room rewrite. Most companies migrate screen by screen with hosting controllers instead, so be ready to discuss both.
Pitfalls

items: Creating the UIKit view in `updateUIView`. It runs on every state change.
Holding a strong reference from the coordinator back to the representable's parent.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: How would you migrate a large UIKit app to SwiftUI incrementally?

A Live Activity shows changing state, such as an order's ETA, on the Lock Screen and in the Dynamic Island. The app defines `ActivityAttributes` (static data) and a `ContentState` (changing data), starts the activity, and updates it locally or through ActivityKit push notifications with the activity's push token.
This connects straight to your live-activity work: the push token goes to the backend, and the server sends updates through APNs.

diagram.title: sequence
diagram.caption: The app only starts the activity and uploads its token. Updates come from your server through APNs, and the system renders them even when the app isn't running. A tap opens `widgetURL`, which your router handles.

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Large `ContentState`. The payload has a strict size limit.
Not ending activities. Stale cards erode user trust.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: Explain the end-to-end flow of a server-updated Live Activity.

Accessibility is part of the definition of done. Combine related elements into one VoiceOver stop, hide decorative images, add custom actions instead of hidden gestures, and support Dynamic Type through text styles.
Accessibility identifiers double as stable hooks for UI tests and Appium automation.
Pitfalls

items: Icon-only buttons with no label. VoiceOver reads the symbol name.
Colour as the only signal for online or offline status.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: How do you audit a screen for accessibility before release?

lessons.title: Signing, TestFlight, App Store and CI

blocks.text: Signing has three parts. A certificate proves who built the app. An App ID with capabilities and entitlements (push, App Groups, Bluetooth background modes) says what it may do. A provisioning profile ties them to devices or to distribution. Automatic signing manages profiles for you, and CI authenticates with an App Store Connect API key instead of a person's login.

A pipeline archives a Release build, exports it with an `ExportOptions.plist` (method `app-store-connect`, destination `upload`), and uploads it to TestFlight. Internal testers get builds immediately, while external testers need a short beta review. Release with phased rollout, which spreads updates over seven days and can be paused, and watch crash rates in Organizer before it reaches everyone.

blocks.code:
# 1. Archive (Release) using an App Store Connect API key
xcodebuild archive \
  -workspace bbInstant.xcworkspace -scheme bbInstant -configuration Release \
  -archivePath build/bbInstant.xcarchive \
  -allowProvisioningUpdates \
  -authenticationKeyPath "$ASC_KEY_PATH" \
  -authenticationKeyID "$ASC_KEY_ID" \
  -authenticationKeyIssuerID "$ASC_ISSUER_ID"

# 2. Export and upload to TestFlight (destination: upload in ExportOptions.plist)
xcodebuild -exportArchive \
  -archivePath build/bbInstant.xcarchive \
  -exportOptionsPlist ExportOptions.plist \
  -exportPath build/export \
  -allowProvisioningUpdates \
  -authenticationKeyPath "$ASC_KEY_PATH" \
  -authenticationKeyID "$ASC_KEY_ID" \
  -authenticationKeyIssuerID "$ASC_ISSUER_ID"

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Committing certificates or API keys to the repo. Keep them in the CI secret store.
Reusing a build number. App Store Connect rejects the upload, so let CI bump it.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: Describe your release process from merge to 100% of users.

links.title: Distributing your app for beta testing and releases

blocks.text: Ask for a permission at the moment it's needed, after a screen that explains why: Bluetooth when the user taps “Find machines nearby”, the camera when they tap “Scan QR”. Every prompt needs its Info.plist purpose string, such as `NSBluetoothAlwaysUsageDescription`, `NSCameraUsageDescription` or `NSFaceIDUsageDescription`. If access was denied, explain what's lost and offer to open Settings with `UIApplication.openSettingsURLString`.

A privacy manifest (`PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy`) declares the data you collect and the approved reason for each required-reason API you use, for example `CA92.1` for UserDefaults that only your app reads. Third-party SDKs ship their own. Protect sensitive screens with LocalAuthentication, and store secrets in the Keychain with access-control flags.
Pitfalls

items: Requesting every permission at first launch. Grant rates drop, and the user can't tell why each one is needed.
Secrets in source code or Info.plist. Anything in the app bundle can be extracted.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: How do you handle a user who denied Bluetooth but needs it to use the machine?

modules.title: iOS 26 and What's New
modules.summary: Liquid Glass, WebView, rich text, on-device AI, App Intents, StoreKit 2, Charts, localisation, rich push, and a WWDC26 watch list.

blocks.text: Recompiling with the iOS 26 SDK gives standard components, such as navigation bars, toolbars, tab bars, sheets and menus, the Liquid Glass look automatically. Your work is mostly removal: drop custom bar backgrounds and opaque materials that now fight the system, and check that content scrolls under the bars as intended.

For your own floating controls, use `glassEffect`. Group nearby glass shapes in a `GlassEffectContainer` so they blend, and give them `glassEffectID`s so one can morph into another. Buttons get `.glass` and `.glassProminent` styles. Tab views gain `tabBarMinimizeBehavior`, a bottom accessory for things like a mini player, and a separate search tab. Use glass for the navigation layer that floats above content, not for content itself.

blocks.caption: LiquidGlass.swift

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Glass on content such as list rows and cards. It's meant for controls and navigation that float above content.
Keeping old custom bar appearances, such as `UINavigationBarAppearance` backgrounds. They hide the new material. Remove them and retest.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: What changes when you rebuild an existing SwiftUI app with the iOS 26 SDK, and what do you have to fix by hand?

links.title: Build a SwiftUI app with the new design

blocks.text: iOS 26 adds a native SwiftUI `WebView` in WebKit, replacing the `WKWebView` representable most apps kept around for terms pages, help centres and payment redirects. For a simple page, pass a URL. For control, create a `WebPage`, an observable object with title, loading state and navigation, and render it with `WebView(page)`.

`TextEditor` now edits an `AttributedString` directly. Bind the text and an `AttributedTextSelection`, and apply formatting with `transformAttributes(in:)`. That's enough for review boxes and notes with bold and italic, with no UIKit text view.

blocks.caption: WebAndRichText.swift

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Keeping a `WKWebView` wrapper plus its delegate code when you only show a page.
Storing rich text as HTML strings. Persist the `AttributedString`, which is `Codable`, or a format your backend owns.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: How would you show a payment provider's web page and detect when it redirects back?

links.title: Code-along: Cook up a rich text experience in SwiftUI with AttributedString

lessons.title: On-device AI with the Foundation Models framework

blocks.text: The Foundation Models framework gives apps the on-device language model behind Apple Intelligence: private, offline and free per request. Always check `SystemLanguageModel.default.availability` first, because devices without Apple Intelligence, or with it switched off, report unavailable, and your UI needs a fallback.

Create a `LanguageModelSession` with instructions, then call `respond(to:)` for text or `respond(to:generating:)` for typed output. `@Generable` structs with `@Guide` constraints make the model return Swift values instead of text you have to parse. `streamResponse` gives partial results as they generate. Tools let the model call your code, such as looking up nearby machines, when it needs facts it doesn't have.

blocks.caption: FoundationModels.swift

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: No availability check. The feature breaks on most devices in the field.
Treating the model as a knowledge base. It's small and on-device, so give it facts through the prompt or tools and keep tasks narrow (summarise, classify, extract).

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: Design a feature that summarises reviews on-device. How do you handle devices where the model isn't available?

Build agentic app experiences with the Foundation Models framework

lessons.title: App Intents: Siri, Shortcuts and interactive widgets

blocks.text: An `AppIntent` is one action your app exposes to the system. The same type powers Siri, the Shortcuts app, Spotlight, Action button, Control Center controls and interactive widget buttons. Declare parameters with `@Parameter`, do the work in `perform()`, and return a dialog or a value.

An `AppShortcutsProvider` makes intents available with zero setup by the user, through spoken phrases that include your app's name. Interactive widgets use `Button(intent:)`, so the action runs without opening the app. In an interview, the key point is that intents are the app's public API to the OS.

blocks.caption: AppIntents.swift

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Heavy UI work in `perform()`. Intents can run in the background with no UI, so return a result and let the app catch up.
Phrases that don't include `\(.applicationName)`. App Shortcut phrases must contain the app name.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: Which actions in a quick-commerce app would you expose as App Intents, and why?

links.title: Develop for Shortcuts and Spotlight with App Intents
Discover new capabilities in the App Intents framework
Build intelligent Siri experiences with App Schemas

blocks.text: StoreKit 2 is async and Swift-native. Load products with `Product.products(for:)`, call `purchase()`, and get back a `VerificationResult`. Unlock content only for verified transactions, and always call `finish()`. Start listening to `Transaction.updates` at launch, because renewals, refunds, Ask to Buy approvals and purchases on other devices arrive there. Restore state from `Transaction.currentEntitlements`.

`SubscriptionStoreView` builds a complete, App Review-friendly paywall for a subscription group, so a custom one is optional. In a SwiftUI file, write `StoreKit.Transaction`, because SwiftUI has its own `Transaction` type. Test with a StoreKit configuration file in Xcode before touching App Store Connect.

diagram.title: flowchart
diagram.caption: Only a verified transaction unlocks anything, and every handled transaction is finished. Renewals, refunds, Ask to Buy approvals and purchases on other devices never come through the button, so a listener started at launch sends them through the same handler.

blocks.caption: StoreKit2.swift

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Unlocking before verification, or forgetting `finish()`. Unfinished transactions are redelivered on every launch.
Listening to `Transaction.updates` only on the paywall screen. Renewals that arrive elsewhere are missed.

blocks.text: Walk through a subscription purchase from tap to unlocked feature, including renewals and refunds.

blocks.text: Swift Charts draws charts from marks (`BarMark`, `LineMark`, `RuleMark`) bound to your data with `.value`. `foregroundStyle(by:)` splits series automatically, and `chartXSelection` adds tap-and-drag inspection with no gesture code. iOS 26 also adds 3D charts with `Chart3D`.

String Catalogs (`.xcstrings`) are Xcode's localisation format. Every `Text("…")` literal and every `String(localized:)` call is extracted automatically when you build. Translators then fill in plural variants such as “1 item” and “3 items”, and device variants, in one file. Add a `comment` to every string, because translators only see the catalog, not your screen.

blocks.caption: ChartsAndLocalization.swift

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Building user-facing strings by concatenation, which breaks word order in other languages. Use interpolation inside one localised string.
Charts with no axis labels or units. The chart may be pretty, but nobody can read it.

blocks.title: Interview check
blocks.text: How do you localise “3 items in your cart” correctly for languages with several plural forms?

links.title: Bring Swift Charts to the third dimension
Explore pie charts and interactivity in Swift Charts

blocks.text: Ask for permission when the value is clear, register for remote notifications, and send the device token to your server (Module 7, lesson 4). Set a `UNUserNotificationCenterDelegate` early. `willPresent` decides how a notification looks while the app is open, and `didReceive` handles taps and action buttons. Route both through the same deep-link parser as everything else. Categories add buttons such as “Reorder” without opening the app.

A Notification Service Extension can change a notification before it's shown: download an image, decrypt the body, or localise the text. The payload must include `mutable-content: 1`, and you have about 30 seconds. If time runs out, `serviceExtensionTimeWillExpire` must deliver your best attempt. `UserNotifications` predates Sendable annotations, hence `@preconcurrency import` in Swift 6.

diagram.title: flowchart
diagram.caption: With `mutable-content: 1` the service extension can attach an image or decrypt the text, with about 30 seconds to do it. A tap reaches `didReceive`, which sends the link to the same router as every other entry point.

blocks.caption: PushNotifications.swift

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: Setting the delegate late, after launch. Taps that launched the app are missed.
Never calling the content handler on a failure path. The notification is then shown unmodified, or late.

blocks.text: Describe the full path of a rich push notification from your server to a tapped deep link.

modules.title: Roadmap deep dives
modules.summary: Four phases from beginner foundations to advanced engineering, each topic with code.

blocks.text: Declarative syntax, simple structures, and how small components react to local data changes.

diagram.title: Phase 1
diagram.caption: UI equals f of state: a tap mutates SwiftUI-owned state, body re-runs, the difference is rendered; a child with a binding writes the same storage.

blocks.text: A tap mutates state that SwiftUI owns; body re-runs and only the difference reaches the screen. A child holding a @Binding reads and writes the same storage.
Text, Image, Button, TextField
Each is a value that describes a piece of UI. `Button` takes an action closure and a label. `TextField` needs a binding, because the text it edits lives somewhere else.
VStack, HStack, ZStack, Spacer, padding
Stacks arrange children on one axis. `ZStack` layers them front to back. `Spacer` absorbs leftover space. `padding` grows the space the view asks for.
.font(), .foregroundStyle(), .background()

Modifiers return a new, wrapped view, so their order changes the result. `foregroundStyle` replaces the older `foregroundColor` and also accepts gradients and hierarchical styles such as `.secondary`.

blocks.code:
Text("Free delivery above ₹199")
    .font(.subheadline.weight(.semibold))
    .foregroundStyle(.green)
    .padding(.horizontal, 12)
    .padding(.vertical, 6)
    .background(.green.opacity(0.12), in: Capsule())   // after padding: the capsule includes it

blocks.text: List and ScrollView
`List` gives system styling, row reuse and swipe actions. `ScrollView` gives you your own look. Use a lazy stack inside it for long content so rows are built only as they scroll in.
Declarative vs imperative: UI = f(State)

In UIKit you change views step by step and must remember every one, which is how a badge ends up stale. In SwiftUI you describe the screen for any state, and SwiftUI works out what changed. Try both modes in the playground.
Value types: why views are structs

A view struct is a cheap, throwaway description. SwiftUI may create it thousands of times while scrolling. The lasting things, the render tree and `@State` storage, are kept by SwiftUI outside your struct.
@State: local read/write memory
`@State` asks SwiftUI to store a value for this view for as long as the view keeps its identity. Writing to it re-runs `body`. Keep it `private`, because only this view should own it.
@Binding: a two-way link to a parent's state
A binding doesn't own anything. It reads and writes someone else's storage. Pass `$value` down, and the child's edits land in the parent's state.
Production layouts, dynamic lists, multi-screen navigation and observable reference-type models.

diagram.title: Phase 2
diagram.caption: Stores injected at the App root are found by any descendant; each tab has its own navigation stack whose path grows when a value is pushed.

blocks.text: Stores created at the App root are injected once and looked up by any descendant. Each tab owns its own NavigationStack, and pushing appends a value to that tab's path.
Section, ForEach, .onDelete, .onMove
`ForEach` generates rows from identifiable data. `onDelete` and `onMove` give you the index offsets to change your array. Swipe-to-delete and the edit-mode handles come for free.
NavigationStack, navigationDestination(for:), TabView

Push values, not views. The destination is chosen by type, in one place. Give each tab its own stack so switching tabs keeps each one's position. `Tab(_:systemImage:)` is iOS 18. On iOS 17, use `.tabItem`.
LazyVStack, LazyHStack, LazyVGrid, LazyHGrid
Lazy containers build children only as they come on screen. A streaming home screen is a lazy vertical list of lazy horizontal rails. A shop grid uses `.adaptive` columns so it fits any width.
Sheets, full-screen covers and alerts

Presentation is state. `sheet(item:)` shows a sheet for a particular value and dismisses when the value becomes nil, so it never shows stale data. Drive alerts from an optional error with a binding that clears it.
Identifiable and Hashable: efficient diffing

SwiftUI matches old and new rows by id. Stable server ids mean a changed title updates one row and an insert animates in. Writing `let id = UUID()` in a model decoded from JSON gives every fetch new ids, so every row is rebuilt.
@Observable data models
Move shared state into an `@Observable` class. SwiftUI tracks which properties each body reads. A view that reads only `items` doesn't re-render when `isSyncing` changes.
.environment() and @Environment
Inject a store once at the root, and any descendant can read it without threading it through every initialiser. The same mechanism serves system values such as `dismiss` and `colorScheme`.
.onAppear and .onDisappear

`onAppear` runs each time a view comes on screen: first show, popping back to it, returning to its tab. Pushing a view over it calls `onDisappear`, and its `.task` is cancelled. Walk through the stack in the playground to see the order.
Animation, custom components, performance tuning and structured system integration.

diagram.title: Phase 3
diagram.caption: Unidirectional flow: the view sends actions to the view model, which calls async services and publishes new state back to the view.

blocks.text: The view only sends actions; the view model is the one place state changes, and async work returns through it.
GeometryReader and the Layout protocol

`GeometryReader` reports the size it was offered, and it takes all of it. Prefer `containerRelativeFrame` for sizes relative to a scroll container, and write a `Layout` when you need your own arrangement.
Animations, matchedGeometryEffect and Canvas

`withAnimation` animates everything a state change affects. `matchedGeometryEffect` makes two views read as one moving view, as with a mini-player expanding. `Canvas` draws immediate-mode paths for charts and waveforms.
UIViewRepresentable and UIViewControllerRepresentable

Wrap UIKit when SwiftUI has no equivalent, such as a Safari sheet, a camera scanner or a legacy chart. `make…` runs once, `update…` runs on every relevant state change, and a `Coordinator` handles delegates.
ViewModifier and ButtonStyle

Package repeated styling once. A `ViewModifier` wraps any view. A `ButtonStyle` also gets the pressed state, so buttons react consistently across the app. This is how a design system ships components.
async/await inside views with .task

`.task(id:)` starts when the view appears, restarts when the id changes, and is cancelled when the view leaves. Cancelled URLSession calls throw `URLError(.cancelled)`, so check `Task.isCancelled` before showing an error.
MVVM and unidirectional data flow
The view sends actions, and the view model is the only place state changes. Here a second tap while paying is ignored by the state machine itself, with no extra `isLoading` flag to forget.
SwiftData for heavy caching and sync

Import large server payloads on a `@ModelActor`, which has its own context off the main actor, and save. Views using `@Query` on the main context update automatically. Upsert by id so a refresh never duplicates rows.
Preference keys: passing values up the tree

The environment sends values down. A `PreferenceKey` sends them up: children publish a value, the key's `reduce` combines them, and an ancestor reads the result. Equal-height plan cards are the classic use.
Optimisation, deep Apple ecosystem integration and low-level control.

diagram.title: Phase 4
diagram.caption: Widgets and Live Activities are rendered by the system: the app writes an App Group store the widget extension reads, and server updates reach Live Activities through APNs.

blocks.text: Widgets and Live Activities run outside your app. The app shares data through an App Group, and the server reaches a Live Activity through APNs; the system renders both.
WidgetKit

A widget is a timeline of snapshots, not a live view. The app writes shared data to an App Group and calls `WidgetCenter.shared.reloadTimelines(ofKind:)`. The extension's provider builds entries from that data.
Live Activities: Lock Screen and Dynamic Island

Start the activity in the app, update it locally or through ActivityKit pushes, and always end it with a final state and a dismissal policy. The layout lives in the widget extension's `ActivityConfiguration`.
Apple Watch apps and complications

watchOS uses the same SwiftUI with a much smaller canvas, so lead with the one number that matters. Complications are WidgetKit widgets in the accessory families. Data reaches the watch through WatchConnectivity or the watch's own network calls.
visionOS: windows, volumes and immersive spaces

A visionOS app declares scenes. A `WindowGroup` is a 2D window in space, the `.volumetric` style makes a bounded 3D volume, and an `ImmersiveSpace` surrounds the user. You open them from the environment.
Diagnosing render loops with Self._printChanges()

Debug builds can log why a body re-ran. A row that reads a whole dictionary of likes re-renders every row on every like. Fix it by passing the one value down, or by giving each post its own observable object.
Combine reactive pipelines
Combine shines for event plumbing that's mostly operators: combine two inputs, transform, de-duplicate and assign. For new UI state, Observation and `async` usually win. Know both.
Custom state engines: a reducer store

Highly dynamic apps such as players, chat and trading benefit from one store per feature: a pure `reduce` function changes state synchronously, and side effects return as new actions. Every change is loggable, replayable and testable.
Thread ownership: who runs where

Write down, for every piece of work, which executor it runs on: the main actor for UI state, an actor for shared mutable caches, the concurrent pool for CPU work, and the system's own queues for networking and AVFoundation. The playground shows what happens to frames when you get it wrong.
