blocks.title: Netflix-style (illustrative design)
blocks.text: Browse dozens of artwork rails, play adaptive video instantly, resume on any device, and download episodes for offline viewing.

diagram.title: Thread map
diagram.caption: Streaming app thread map: UI state on the main actor, caches and progress on actors, decoding and downloads in AVFoundation and background sessions.

blocks.text: Who runs where

rows: UI state must be mutated on main; views read @Observable models.
AVPlayer manages its pipeline; you only observe it.
One cache, de-duplicated requests, decoding off main.
Batches writes so a seek storm doesn't become a network storm.
Keeps downloading after the app is suspended or killed.

blocks.text: Player state you can observe safely

AVPlayer runs on its own threads and reports back through KVO and time observers. Deliver time updates on the main queue, then tell the compiler you're already isolated with `MainActor.assumeIsolated`. Remove the observer when playback stops, or it keeps firing.
Smooth scrolling across 40 rails

Nest lazy stacks so only visible posters exist. Give every item a stable server id. Downsample artwork to the poster size off the main thread, and share one image actor so two rails showing the same title make one request. Prefetch the next rail's first images when a rail appears.
Resume where you left off

Time updates arrive twice a second, but the server only needs the latest position every few seconds. An actor keeps the newest value per episode and flushes on a timer, on pause and when the app goes to the background. A failed flush keeps the value for the next try, unless a newer one has arrived.
Offline downloads that survive app exit

HLS downloads use an `AVAssetDownloadURLSession` with a background configuration, so the system keeps downloading when the app is suspended. Persist the task-to-episode mapping, because the delegate reconnects to running tasks on relaunch. Respect storage limits and expire licences on schedule.
DRM, background audio and Picture in Picture

Protected streams use FairPlay through `AVContentKeySession`: the app asks your key server for a licence when the player requests one. Set the audio session category to `.playback` and enable the Audio background mode so sound continues on the Lock Screen. `AVPictureInPictureController`, or `VideoPlayer`'s built-in support, keeps video floating when the user leaves the app.
Interview prompts

items: Design the home screen. How do you keep 120 Hz scrolling with 40 rails of artwork?
Where does each piece of work run while a video plays?
How do you make resume position correct across two devices?

blocks.title: YouTube-style (illustrative design)
blocks.text: An endless feed with autoplaying muted previews, uploads that keep going after the app closes, and live comment and like counts.

diagram.title: Thread map
diagram.caption: Video platform thread map: feed paging and one shared preview player on the main actor; uploads run in a background session whose progress returns to the main actor.

blocks.text: Who runs where

rows: Guard and flag are set without a suspension in between, so no double loads.
A player per cell would exhaust decoders and memory.
Continues after suspension; the app is relaunched for events.
Delegate callbacks are not on main; hop before touching UI state.

blocks.text: Only one preview plays at a time

Give every cell a visibility callback and keep a single coordinator that owns one player. The most visible cell wins. A cell scrolling away pauses only if it's the one playing. `onScrollVisibilityChange` is iOS 18. On iOS 17, compute visibility from geometry.
Infinite feed without duplicate loads

Ask for the next page a few rows before the end. Because the pager is `@MainActor`, the `isLoading` check and set can't interleave with another call; that only happens at an `await`. Drop items you already have, because a cursor can repeat items when the feed changes underneath.
Uploads that survive the app closing

Background sessions upload from a *file*, never from memory. The system runs the transfer, and if the app was killed it relaunches it to deliver events. Store the session's completion handler from `application(_:handleEventsForBackgroundURLSession:completionHandler:)` and call it when `urlSessionDidFinishEvents` fires.
Live counts without hammering the server

Poll a lightweight counts endpoint only while the video is on screen, back off when the counts stop changing, and stop in the background. Switch to a WebSocket only when the experience needs true real time, such as a live stream chat. Likes are optimistic: update the count immediately and roll back if the request fails.
Interview prompts

items: Why one shared player instead of one per cell?
Walk through an upload when the user kills the app at 40%.
How do you prevent two page loads firing at once?

blocks.title: Quick-commerce / marketplace (illustrative design)
blocks.text: Search a large catalogue, keep one consistent cart across every screen, check out exactly once, and keep prices and stock fresh.

diagram.title: Thread map
diagram.caption: E-commerce thread map: catalog, cart and checkout state on the main actor; token refresh in an actor; the payment SDK runs its own UI and calls back through a continuation.

blocks.text: Who runs where

rows: One writer for state that several screens display.
Each keystroke cancels the previous request automatically.
Wrapped with a checked continuation and resumed exactly once.
Grid scrolling never decodes on main.

blocks.text: A cart that survives rapid taps

Update the cart optimistically so the badge responds instantly, then reconcile with the server, which may clamp to stock. Rapid taps send requests that can return out of order. Give each request a ticket per SKU and ignore any response that a newer tap has superseded.
Charging exactly once

Network failures happen after the server has charged the card, so a retry must not create a second order. Create one idempotency key per checkout attempt and reuse it on every retry. The server returns the original order for a repeated key. Make a new key only after success. Combine this with the checkout state machine so a double tap can't start a second attempt.
Fresh prices and stock without refetching everything

Treat price and stock as short-lived. Refresh the cart when the app returns to the foreground and before showing checkout. Use ETags for catalogue pages. If the server reports a changed price at checkout, show the difference and ask for confirmation instead of failing silently.
Search as you type

`.task(id: query)` restarts on every keystroke, and the previous task's sleep throws when it's cancelled, so stale requests never land. Keep the last results on screen while the new query loads, so the list doesn't flash empty. Covered in depth in Module 15, lesson 2.
Interview prompts

items: Two taps on + return out of order. What does the badge show?
The network dies after the card was charged. What prevents a second charge?
Where does the payment SDK's callback run, and how do you get back to the UI?

blocks.title: Feed + chat (illustrative design)
blocks.text: An image-heavy feed with instant likes, real-time chat that never loses or reorders a message, and push notifications that open the right screen.

diagram.title: Thread map
diagram.caption: Social app thread map: per-post observable models on the main actor; the chat socket and the outbox are actors; the outbox is persisted so messages survive offline periods.

blocks.text: Who runs where

rows: Main actor, one object per post
A like re-renders one row, not the feed.
Full-size photos never decode on main or into memory.
Ordered delivery; survives offline and app restarts.
One parser for links, pushes and Live Activity taps.

blocks.text: Instant likes that stay correct

Give each post its own `@Observable` object, so a like re-renders one row. Update the count optimistically and roll back if the request fails. Take the server's count when it answers, so concurrent likes from other users are reflected.
A chat outbox that never loses or reorders

Messages are written to the outbox first, so they appear immediately with a “sending” state, then flushed in order. A message is removed only after the server acknowledges it. A failure stops the flush, and the rest wait for the reconnect. The `flushing` flag is the reentrancy guard: while one flush awaits, a new enqueue appends and returns, and the running flush picks it up. The client id lets the server drop duplicates after a retry.
Image-heavy feeds without memory spikes
A 12-megapixel photo decodes to about 48 MB. Downsample to the displayed size with ImageIO, decode immediately while still off the main thread, and cache the small result.
Ordering, typing indicators and push routing

Order messages by the server's sequence number, never the device clock, and insert by sequence when late messages arrive after a reconnect. Throttle typing indicators to one event every few seconds. Parse every notification tap into the same `Route` enum used for deep links (Module 7, lesson 2), so a push opens the right chat whether the app is running, in the background or launched cold.
Interview prompts

items: How do you guarantee chat messages are delivered in order, exactly once?
A user likes a post twice quickly while offline. What happens?
Why does a feed of photos crash with memory warnings, and how do you fix it?

questions.q: What is the difference between let and var?
questions.a: `let` binds a constant that can't be reassigned; `var` can be. On a struct, `let` freezes the whole value. On a class instance only the reference is fixed, and its properties can still change.

questions.q: What is an optional and how is it implemented?
questions.a: `Optional<Wrapped>` is an enum with `.none` and `.some(Wrapped)`. `nil` is `.none`. The compiler makes you unwrap it before use, so a missing value is handled explicitly.

questions.q: if let vs guard let: when do you use each?
questions.a: `if let` scopes the unwrapped value to its block. `guard let` requires an early exit when nil and keeps the value for the rest of the scope. That suits preconditions at the top of a function.
`map` transforms each element. `compactMap` transforms and drops nils. `flatMap` flattens a sequence of sequences. On an Optional, `flatMap` chains a transform that itself returns an optional.
A closure that outlives the function call because it is stored or called asynchronously. It must be marked `@escaping`. Non-escaping is the default: it's cheaper and allows implicit `self`.
By reference by default, so they see later changes. A capture list such as `[count]` copies the value when the closure is created. `[weak self]` avoids a strong reference to the owner.
Binary floating point can't represent values like 0.1 exactly, so rounding errors accumulate. Use `Decimal` or integer minor units (paise), and format with a currency format style.

questions.q: What are key paths and where are they useful?
questions.a: Typed references to properties, such as `\Item.price`. They work as functions in `map(\.name)`, in sort descriptors, in SwiftData `@Query` sorts and predicates, in dynamic member lookup, and in SwiftUI bindings.
It runs its block when the current scope exits, however it exits (return, throw, break). Multiple defers run in reverse order. Use it for cleanup such as unlocking or closing files.

questions.q: throws vs Result vs returning an optional?
questions.a: `throws` propagates a reason with `try`. `Result` stores success or failure as a value, which is useful for callbacks and caching outcomes. An optional loses the reason for failure.

Structs are value types: copied, no inheritance, memberwise init, no deinit. Classes are reference types: shared identity, inheritance, deinit, `===`. Prefer structs unless you need shared mutable identity.

questions.q: When do you choose a class?
questions.a: When you need shared identity (a socket session), inheritance (UIKit subclasses), Objective-C interop, or deinit-based cleanup. If that shared state is accessed concurrently, consider an actor.
Designing around protocols and protocol extensions with default implementations, composing capabilities instead of inheriting from base classes. It works for structs and enums, not just classes.

questions.q: Explain dispatch for protocol extension methods.
questions.a: Methods declared as protocol requirements dispatch dynamically through the witness table. Methods that exist only in an extension dispatch statically on the variable's declared type, so a conformer's own implementation is skipped when called through the protocol.

`some P` is an opaque type: one concrete type, known to the compiler, with no box. `any P` is an existential box that can hold different types at runtime, with dynamic dispatch and possible allocation. Prefer `some`.
A placeholder type inside a protocol that each conformer fills in, such as `Element` in `Collection`. It makes the protocol generic over that type.
Declared as `protocol Repository<Entity>`, they let you write constrained types like `some Collection<Int>` or `any Repository<Product>` without generic where-clauses.
A struct or enum method that changes `self` must be marked `mutating`. You can't call it on a `let` constant.
It prevents subclassing, which lets the compiler use static dispatch and inline calls. It also documents that the class isn't designed for inheritance.
If every stored property is Codable, the compiler generates `CodingKeys`, `init(from:)` and `encode(to:)`. You can override the key mapping only, or write the initialiser by hand.
A type with a `wrappedValue` (and optionally a `projectedValue`, exposed as `$name`) applied with `@Name` to encapsulate storage logic. `@State`, `@Binding` and `@AppStorage` are property wrappers.
A type marked `@resultBuilder` that turns a sequence of statements into one value through `buildBlock`, `buildEither`, `buildOptional` and similar methods. `@ViewBuilder` is the best-known one.

Automatic Reference Counting. The compiler inserts retain and release calls, and an object is freed when its strong reference count reaches zero. It is deterministic and not a tracing garbage collector.
Two or more objects holding strong references to each other, so no count reaches zero. Typical case: a view model stores a closure on a child object, and the closure captures the view model strongly.
`weak` is optional and becomes nil when the object is freed. `unowned` is non-optional and assumes the object outlives the reference. Accessing it after deallocation crashes.

questions.q: Can a Task cause a retain cycle?
questions.a: A Task strongly captures what it uses until it finishes. That only becomes a cycle when self also stores the task and the task never ends, for example an infinite loop. Use weak captures for long-running loops.
Value types such as Array share storage between copies and duplicate it only on mutation when the buffer isn't uniquely referenced, which is checked with `isKnownUniquelyReferenced`.

questions.q: How do you find a memory leak?
questions.a: Check deinit logs, then use the Xcode Memory Graph to look at retain paths, and Instruments Leaks or Allocations with generational marks while repeating the flow. Look for objects whose count grows every time.
The owner holds the child strongly. If the child held its delegate (the owner) strongly too, you'd have a cycle. The protocol is constrained to `AnyObject` so it can be weak.

questions.q: Stack vs heap for Swift values?
questions.a: Value types are often stack-allocated, but they get boxed on the heap when captured by escaping closures, stored in large existentials, or marked indirect. Classes always live on the heap with atomic refcounting.

questions.q: What dispatch mechanisms does Swift use?
questions.a: Static (structs, final, private, extension-only methods), vtable (overridable class methods), witness table (protocol requirements) and Objective-C message send (`@objc dynamic`).

questions.q: What is a View in SwiftUI?
questions.a: A lightweight value that describes a piece of UI through its `body`. SwiftUI keeps the real render tree and diffs new descriptions against it, so creating views is cheap.
Each modifier wraps the view in a new view. `.padding().background()` paints the padded area; `.background().padding()` paints only the content and adds space outside.
An opaque return type. `body` returns one concrete, often deeply nested generic type that the compiler infers, and you don't have to spell it.
When a dependency it read changes: `@State`, an observed property, an environment value, or the view's inputs from its parent. It then diffs the result.
A result builder that lets `body` and closures contain several views, `if`/`else` and `switch`, producing `TupleView` or conditional content.
Narrower dependencies, reuse and readability. SwiftUI can skip a subview's body when its inputs haven't changed, which computed properties inside a parent can't offer.

questions.q: How do you support Dynamic Type?
questions.a: Use text styles rather than fixed sizes, use `@ScaledMetric` for spacing and icons, let text wrap, and test at the largest accessibility sizes.
It erases type information, so SwiftUI loses structural identity and diffs less efficiently. Prefer `@ViewBuilder`, `Group` or conditional content.

The parent proposes a size, the child chooses its own size based on that proposal, and the parent places the child within its coordinate space. Modifiers like `frame` and `padding` change the proposal.
`@State` is a source of truth owned by a view and preserved across body runs. `@Binding` is a read-write reference to state owned by someone else.

`@Observable` tracks which properties each body reads and invalidates only those views. `ObservableObject` invalidates every observer on any `@Published` change and needs `@StateObject`/`@ObservedObject`.

`@StateObject` creates and owns the object for the view's lifetime. `@ObservedObject` only observes one passed in. Creating an object in `@ObservedObject` can recreate it whenever the parent re-renders.
It produces bindings to properties of an `@Observable` object you don't own via `@State`, for example `$model.name` in a TextField.
Values flow down the view tree implicitly. Read them with `@Environment(\.key)` or `@Environment(Model.self)` and set them with `.environment(...)`. Missing observable objects crash at runtime.

Structural identity is a view's type and position in the hierarchy, including which branch of an if it's in. Explicit identity comes from `ForEach` ids or `.id()`. Identity decides state lifetime and transitions.
When `x` changes, SwiftUI treats the view as a new one: it discards its state, restarts `.task` and `onAppear`, and runs transitions. Useful for resetting a form, harmful with unstable values.

questions.q: Why is creating a view model in a view's init risky?
questions.a: The init runs every time the parent re-renders. Even with `State(initialValue:)` only the first instance is kept, but the object is still constructed each time, along with any side effects.

questions.q: What is a single source of truth?
questions.a: Each piece of data has one owner. Everything else reads it, derives from it or binds to it, so there are no copies to keep in sync.

questions.q: How do you share state between unrelated screens?
questions.a: Lift it into an `@Observable` model owned by a common ancestor or the App, and pass it by environment or init. For data that outlives the session, back it with a persisted service.
`List` gives platform styling, cell reuse, swipe actions, selection and refresh. `LazyVStack` in a ScrollView gives a custom look and lazy creation without the same recycling.

questions.q: Why must ForEach data be identifiable?
questions.a: SwiftUI uses ids to match rows across updates for inserts, deletes, moves, animations and preserved state. Unstable ids cause wrong animations and state bleeding between rows.
Indices shift when items are inserted or removed, so identity is wrong, and bindings to removed indices can crash.

`Grid` builds every cell eagerly and aligns real rows and columns. `LazyVGrid` builds cells lazily for large scrolling collections, with column definitions only.

questions.q: How do you paginate a list?

questions.q: How do you add pull to refresh?
questions.a: Attach `.refreshable { await reload() }` to a List or ScrollView. The spinner stays visible until the async work finishes.

questions.q: How do you handle deep links?
questions.a: Receive the URL in `onOpenURL` (or a notification handler), parse it into your Route enum in one place, then mutate the router's path. Universal links also need associated domains.

questions.q: How does a coordinator work in SwiftUI?
questions.a: A Router or Coordinator object owns the path and presentation state and exposes intent methods (`showMachine(id:)`). Views call it instead of knowing destinations, so navigation is testable.
`sheet(item:)` presents for a specific Identifiable value and dismisses when it becomes nil, which avoids showing stale data. Use it whenever the sheet depends on a selection.

questions.q: How does a view dismiss itself?
questions.a: Read `@Environment(\.dismiss) private var dismiss` and call `dismiss()`. It works for sheets and pushed views.

`.animation(_:value:)` animates a subtree when a given value changes. `withAnimation` wraps a state change and animates every view that depends on it.

questions.q: How do you respect Reduce Motion?

questions.q: How do you make a view model testable?
questions.a: Inject dependencies through protocols, avoid singletons and global state, expose state as an Equatable enum, and make actions async so tests can await them.

questions.q: Why model screen state as an enum?
questions.a: Impossible combinations such as loading plus error can't exist, and the view's switch is checked for exhaustiveness.

questions.q: Compare MVC, MVVM, VIPER and TCA.
questions.a: MVC tends toward massive view controllers. MVVM separates presentation logic. VIPER enforces strict roles at the cost of boilerplate. TCA uses unidirectional reducers with strong testability and a dependency on the library.

questions.q: Where does navigation live in MVVM?
questions.a: In a router or coordinator. The view model calls a router protocol or emits an intent, and views stay unaware of destinations.

questions.q: What is a singleton and what are its drawbacks?
questions.a: One shared instance behind a private init. Drawbacks: hidden global state, tight coupling, hard to replace in tests, and stale state across logouts. Mitigate by injecting it through a protocol.
One object hands decisions or events to another through a protocol, as in UITableViewDelegate. The delegate reference is weak to avoid a cycle.
NotificationCenter (app-wide, loosely coupled), KVO (Objective-C properties), Combine publishers, Observation (`@Observable`) and AsyncStream. Choose by scope and coupling.

An adapter converts one interface into the one your code expects, such as wrapping a vendor SDK. A facade gives a simple interface over a complex subsystem.

questions.q: What is the Decorator pattern in Swift?
questions.a: A type that wraps another conforming to the same protocol and adds behaviour such as logging, caching or auth, which you compose at the composition root.

questions.q: What does the Repository pattern give you?
questions.a: One protocol for data access that hides whether data comes from the network, a cache or a database, so domain and view models don't know about URLSession or SwiftData.
Less often than in Java, because default arguments and memberwise inits cover most cases. SwiftUI modifiers and request builders are builder-like.

questions.q: How do you implement the State pattern in Swift?
questions.a: An enum of states with a `mutating func handle(_ event:)` transition function. Illegal states are unrepresentable, and illegal transitions are handled in one place.

questions.q: What are the risks of DispatchSemaphore?

Operations add dependencies, cancellation state, KVO-observable status and `maxConcurrentOperationCount`. GCD is lighter and lower level.

questions.q: How do you make a class thread-safe?
questions.a: Route all access to mutable state through one mechanism: a serial queue, a lock (NSLock, Mutex) or an actor. Every read and write path must go through it.

questions.q: Why must UI updates happen on the main thread?
questions.a: UIKit and SwiftUI aren't thread-safe, and the main run loop drives event handling and rendering. Background UI updates cause glitches and crashes.

questions.q: What does async/await improve over completion handlers?
questions.a: Linear control flow, error propagation with `try`, no forgotten or double callbacks, built-in cancellation, and compiler-checked isolation.
A unit of asynchronous work. `Task { }` inherits the current actor, priority and task-locals. `Task.detached` inherits none of them.
`async let` suits a fixed, small number of concurrent child tasks. `withTaskGroup` suits a dynamic number of children.
Child tasks are bound to their parent's scope. The parent waits for them, errors and cancellation propagate, and no task outlives its scope by accident.

A marker that a type is safe to pass across concurrency domains: value types with Sendable members, actors, and immutable final classes. `@unchecked Sendable` is a manual promise.

questions.q: What does Swift 6 language mode change?
questions.a: Data-race checks become errors. You migrate module by module. Swift 6.2 adds approachable concurrency: an option for default MainActor isolation, and `@concurrent` to opt work onto the concurrent pool.

questions.q: How do you bridge a callback API to async?

questions.q: data vs download vs upload tasks?
questions.a: Data tasks return the body in memory. Download tasks write to a file and can run in background sessions. Upload tasks send a body or file.

questions.q: How do you design a network layer?
questions.a: A typed Endpoint describing request and response, a generic APIClient protocol, an error enum, decoding, decorators for auth, logging and retry, and injection into features.

questions.q: How do you handle 401s and token refresh?
questions.a: Use a single-flight refresh actor, retry the original request once with the new token, and sign the user out only when the refresh itself is rejected.

questions.q: What is a good retry strategy?
questions.a: Retry only transient, idempotent failures, with exponential backoff and jitter, a cap on attempts, respect for `Retry-After`, and cancellation-aware sleeps.

questions.q: How do you map JSON keys with Codable?
questions.a: Use a `CodingKeys` enum with raw values, or `keyDecodingStrategy = .convertFromSnakeCase`. Don't combine the two.

questions.q: How do you handle missing JSON fields?
questions.a: Use optional properties, or `decodeIfPresent` with a default in a custom init. Decide for each field whether missing data is an error.

questions.q: How do you test networking code?
questions.a: Fake the APIClient protocol for feature tests. Test the real client with a URLProtocol stub on an ephemeral session, and assert on both the request and the error mapping.

questions.q: How do you cancel in-flight requests?
questions.a: Cancel the Task that awaits them. Async URLSession methods respond to cancellation and throw. In SwiftUI, `.task` cancels for you.

questions.q: Unit vs integration vs UI tests?
questions.a: Unit tests isolate logic with fakes. Integration tests combine real components such as client and decoder. UI tests drive the running app through XCUITest.

questions.q: How do you mock dependencies in Swift?
questions.a: Put dependencies behind protocols (or structs of closures) and write fakes that return scripted results and record calls. No runtime mocking library is needed.

questions.q: How do you test async code?
questions.a: Write async test functions and await the code. Use `confirmation()` in Swift Testing, or XCTestExpectation with `fulfillment(of:)`, for callbacks.

questions.q: How do you test a view model's state transitions?
questions.a: Inject fakes you can suspend and resume (for example with continuations), then assert the state at each step: loading, then loaded or failed.

questions.a: Add `let _ = Self._printChanges()` in debug builds, use the SwiftUI instrument's cause-and-effect view, then narrow what each body reads.

questions.q: How do you improve launch time?

questions.q: How do you reduce image memory?

questions.q: How do you symbolicate a crash?

questions.a: Feature and core packages with explicit dependencies give faster incremental builds, enforced boundaries through access control, and isolated previews and tests.

questions.q: What are the basics of code signing?
questions.a: A certificate identifies the developer, an App ID identifies the app, and a provisioning profile ties them to devices and entitlements. Xcode can manage this automatically.

questions.q: What is the SwiftUI app lifecycle?
questions.a: An `@main` App struct declares Scenes such as WindowGroup. `scenePhase` reports state changes, and `UIApplicationDelegateAdaptor` handles push and other app-delegate callbacks.

Request permission, register for remote notifications, receive the APNs device token, send it to your server, and the server sends payloads through APNs. A notification service extension can modify content on arrival.

questions.q: What do you get for free when you rebuild with the iOS 26 SDK?
questions.a: Standard bars, tab bars, toolbars, sheets and menus adopt Liquid Glass automatically. Your job is mostly removing custom backgrounds that fight it and checking content under the bars.

questions.q: When should you apply glassEffect yourself?
questions.a: For your own floating controls in the navigation layer, such as a custom control cluster or a map overlay. Group nearby ones in a GlassEffectContainer. Don't put glass on content such as rows and cards.

questions.q: How does the SwiftUI WebView in iOS 26 differ from wrapping WKWebView?
questions.a: It's a native SwiftUI view. For control you pair it with an observable WebPage (title, loading, navigation), so there's no UIViewRepresentable and no delegate boilerplate.

questions.q: How do you check whether the on-device model can be used?
questions.a: Read SystemLanguageModel.default.availability, and fall back gracefully when it's unavailable: the device isn't eligible, Apple Intelligence is off, or the model isn't ready.

questions.q: What does @Generable give you in Foundation Models?
questions.a: The model produces a typed Swift value matching the struct's schema, constrained by @Guide descriptions and rules, instead of free text you have to parse.

questions.q: What are tools in the Foundation Models framework?
questions.a: Types conforming to Tool that the model can call during a response to get facts or perform actions. Their arguments are @Generable, and the session decides when to call them.

questions.q: Why are App Intents important beyond Siri?
questions.a: One intent powers Siri, Shortcuts, Spotlight, the Action button, Control Center and interactive widget buttons. It's your app's public API to the system.

questions.q: What must every StoreKit 2 purchase flow do?
questions.a: Verify the transaction, unlock only on .verified, call finish(), and listen to Transaction.updates from launch for renewals, refunds and Ask to Buy.

questions.q: Why write StoreKit.Transaction in a SwiftUI file?
questions.a: SwiftUI has its own Transaction type for animations, so the bare name is ambiguous. The compiler reports it as an error.

questions.q: How do String Catalogs handle plurals?
questions.a: The catalog stores variants per plural category for each language, such as one and other (plus few or many where a language needs them), for one interpolated string like "\(count) items".

questions.q: What can a Notification Service Extension do, and what are its limits?
questions.a: Modify content before display (attach media, decrypt, localise) when the payload has mutable-content: 1. It has about 30 seconds, and serviceExtensionTimeWillExpire must deliver a best attempt.

questions.q: How do you route a notification tap to the right screen?
questions.a: Handle didReceive in UNUserNotificationCenterDelegate (set early at launch), read the deep link from userInfo, and pass it to the same router used for URLs and Live Activity taps.
